# How to use this guide

Applied Biochemistry is a second-semester subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum (2 credits, 40 hours, including a few laboratory observation hours). It is examined in a **combined university paper with Applied Nutrition and Dietetics**: Applied Biochemistry is **Section A (25 marks)** and Applied Nutrition and Dietetics is **Section B (50 marks)** of one 3-hour, 75-mark paper. Biochemistry explains what happens to food after it is eaten, so study it alongside the Nutrition pack — carbohydrates, lipids and proteins appear in both.

**How the units are arranged.** The INC syllabus has eight units. Units VI and VII are small and closely linked (bilirubin is part of the liver function tests), so they share one notes file:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Carbohydrates, blood glucose and diabetes | I | 8 |
| Unit 2 Lipids, lipoproteins and atherosclerosis | II | 8 |
| Unit 3 Amino acids, proteins and plasma proteins | III | 9 |
| Unit 4 Clinical enzymology | IV | 4 |
| Unit 5 Acid–base balance | V | 3 |
| Unit 6 Heme catabolism, jaundice and organ function tests | VI + VII | 2 + 3 |
| Unit 7 Immunochemistry | VIII | 3 |

Study one notes file a day: read it, write out the pathways and tables once from memory, then answer the questions and MCQs for that unit without looking. Unit 1 is long because it carries the most hours and the most questions.

**Section A: Applied Biochemistry (25 marks)** — as given in INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3. There is **no essay** in this section and **no internal choice**, so every question must be answered. Your university may print it differently; confirm with your university.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 4 multiple-choice questions | 4 × 1 = 4 |
| Short | 3 short answers | 3 × 5 = 15 |
| Very short | 3 very short answers | 3 × 2 = 6 |
| **Total** | | **25** |

Section A is one third of the 3-hour paper, so the mock test here is timed at 60 minutes. The university exam is 75 marks (Biochemistry 25 + Nutrition 50) with 25 internal marks. You must pass theory with at least 50%. Because the paper is combined, a weak Biochemistry section can pull down the whole result — do not leave it for the last week.

**About the long questions in the bank.** INC lists "essay" as an assessment method for Units I–IV, so long (10-mark) questions are included for practice and for internal/sessional tests. In the university paper, expect the same topics to come as 5-mark short answers; a long answer cut to its main points makes a good short answer.

**Laboratory values.** Normal values in these notes are approximate ("about") and are the figures most Indian textbooks use. Every laboratory prints its own reference range, which depends on its method; in the exam, write "about" or give the range your teacher taught.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a favourite; comes up in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer with a table or pathway.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and the usual style of nursing biochemistry papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Regulation of blood glucose, OGTT (procedure and curves), types of GTT, diabetes types and complications, HbA1c, hypoglycaemia causes, glycolysis |
| 2 | Classification of fatty acids, essential and trans fatty acids, ketone bodies, lipoproteins, lipid profile values, compounds from cholesterol, atherosclerosis |
| 3 | Essential amino acids, urea cycle, phenylketonuria/alkaptonuria/albinism, plasma proteins and their functions, causes of proteinuria and hypoproteinaemia, electrophoresis patterns |
| 4 | Isoenzymes (definition, properties, CK and LDH), cardiac markers in MI, liver enzymes, ALP, PSA |
| 5 | Normal pH and ABG values, buffers, renal regulation, types and causes of acid–base disorders |
| 6 | Haem breakdown pathway, types of jaundice with lab findings, van den Bergh test, normal values of RFT, LFT and TFT |
| 7 | Structure of immunoglobulin (with diagram), classes and functions, ELISA principle and interpretation |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Use tables and flow charts.** Comparisons (type 1 vs type 2 diabetes, three types of jaundice, lipoproteins, immunoglobulin classes, acid–base disorders) score well as tables. Pathways (haem breakdown, urea cycle outline, fat digestion) should be written as arrow chains.
2. **Quote normal values with units and the word "about"**: fasting glucose 70–100 mg/dL, pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, HCO3⁻ 22–26 mmol/L, bilirubin 0.2–1.2 mg/dL, total protein 6–8 g/dL, albumin 3.5–5 g/dL, urea 15–40 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL, total cholesterol below 200 mg/dL.
3. **Draw** the immunoglobulin Y structure, GTT curves, the electrophoresis pattern and the time-course of cardiac markers; a neat labelled figure earns marks quickly.
4. Every answer should end with **one or two nursing points** — sample collection (fluoride tube, avoid haemolysis, fresh urine), patient preparation (OGTT, lipid profile), and what to observe (hypoglycaemia, Kussmaul breathing, jaundice in newborns).
5. For 2-mark answers write a definition plus one example or one value. For 5-mark answers write 6–8 clear points or a table with a short introduction.
6. MCQs come from small facts: enzyme names, which test detects what, which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta. Read the "Remember" list of each notes file the night before.
7. With only 25 marks in 60 minutes, spend about 1–2 minutes on each MCQ, 10–12 minutes on each short answer and 4–5 minutes on each very short answer.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, write these once from memory: the **haem breakdown chain**, the **three types of jaundice table**, the **OGTT procedure and curves**, the **immunoglobulin Y diagram**, and the **ABG normal values**. Then read the tables below. All values are approximate ("about"); labs print their own ranges.

**Normal values to quote**

| Test | About |
| --- | --- |
| Fasting plasma glucose | 70–100 mg/dL; diabetes ≥ 126 |
| 2-h OGTT | below 140 normal; 140–199 IGT; ≥ 200 diabetes |
| HbA1c | below 5.7% normal; ≥ 6.5% diabetes |
| Renal threshold for glucose | 180 mg/dL |
| Total cholesterol / LDL / HDL / TG | below 200 / below 100 / above 40 (men), 50 (women) / below 150 mg/dL |
| Total protein / albumin / globulin | 6–8 / 3.5–5 / 2–3.5 g/dL; A:G above 1 |
| Blood pH | 7.35–7.45 |
| PaCO2 / HCO3⁻ / PaO2 | 35–45 mmHg / 22–26 mmol/L / 80–100 mmHg |
| Anion gap | 8–16 mmol/L |
| Serum bilirubin total / direct | 0.2–1.2 / up to 0.3 mg/dL; jaundice visible above 2–3 |
| Blood urea / creatinine / uric acid | 15–40 / 0.6–1.2 / 3.5–7 mg/dL |
| GFR / urine volume / specific gravity | about 120 mL/min / 1–2 L per day / 1.003–1.030 |
| Proteinuria | above 150 mg/day; microalbuminuria 30–300 mg/day |
| TSH | 0.4–4.5 mIU/L |
| PSA | above about 4 ng/mL needs work-up |

**Unit by unit**

| Unit | Must-know facts |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Carbohydrates | End products glucose, fructose, galactose; SGLT-1 (glucose + Na — basis of ORS); glycolysis net 2 ATP, no O2 needed; insulin the only glucose-lowering hormone; type 1 autoimmune/absolute deficiency, type 2 insulin resistance; DKA = ketones + acidosis; OGTT: 3 days normal diet, overnight fast, 75 g glucose in 250–300 mL water, samples up to 2 h; lag curve (gastrectomy, hyperthyroid), flat curve (malabsorption, hypothyroid, Addison's), renal glycosuria; mini GTT = fasting + 2 h; GCT = 50 g, non-fasting, 1 h; HbA1c = glycated Hb, 2–3 months' average; hypoglycaemia below 70, Whipple's triad |
| 2 Lipids | MUFA one double bond (oleic); PUFA linoleic, linolenic, arachidonic; essential FA linoleic + α-linolenic (deficiency phrynoderma); trans fat ↑ LDL ↓ HDL; bile salts emulsify, pancreatic lipase digests; chylomicrons in lymph; β-oxidation in mitochondria with carnitine; ketone bodies acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone (Rothera's misses β-HB); cholesterol → bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D3; chylomicron dietary fat, VLDL liver fat, LDL bad, HDL good; LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5; atherosclerosis: foam cells → fatty streak → plaque |
| 3 Proteins | Essential: PVT TIM HALL (arginine, histidine semi-essential); leucine and lysine purely ketogenic; pepsin, trypsin (enteropeptidase), rennin; transamination needs B6; urea cycle only in liver; glycine → haem, creatine; tyrosine → catecholamines, thyroxine, melanin; tryptophan → serotonin, niacin; PKU (mousy odour), alkaptonuria (urine blackens), albinism (tyrosinase); albumin keeps oncotic pressure; Bence Jones in myeloma; electrophoresis pH 8.6 — albumin fastest; M band myeloma; β–γ bridging cirrhosis; α2 ↑ nephrotic |
| 4 Enzymes | Isoenzymes: same reaction, different structure, mobility, tissue, Km, heat stability; CK-MB heart, MM muscle, BB brain; LDH-1 heart (flip after MI), LDH-5 liver; ALT most liver-specific; ALP + GGT ↑↑ obstruction; GGT ↑ alcohol; MI: troponin (best, stays 7–14 days), CK-MB (normal in 2–3 days), AST, LDH (last); CK and aldolase in muscle disease (Duchenne); ALP in rickets, Paget's; PSA and tartrate-labile ACP in prostate cancer |
| 5 Acid–base | pH = −log [H⁺]; buffers (seconds) → lungs (minutes) → kidneys (days); bicarbonate main blood buffer, Hb for CO2, phosphate in urine; HCO3⁻ : H2CO3 = 20 : 1; kidney reabsorbs HCO3⁻, excretes titratable acid and NH4⁺; ROME; met. acidosis — DKA, lactic, renal failure, diarrhoea; met. alkalosis — vomiting, NG aspiration, diuretics; resp. acidosis — COPD, respiratory depression; resp. alkalosis — hyperventilation, altitude |
| 6 Haem, jaundice, function tests | RBC 120 days → haem → biliverdin → bilirubin (on albumin) → liver conjugation (UDP-glucuronyl transferase) → bile → urobilinogen → stercobilin; haemolytic: indirect ↑, no urine bilirubin, urobilinogen ↑; obstructive: direct ↑, urine bilirubin +, urobilinogen absent, clay stool, ALP ↑↑; hepatic: biphasic, ALT/AST ↑↑; Fouchet's (pigments), Hay's (salts), Ehrlich's (urobilinogen); TSH best thyroid screen |
| 7 Immunochemistry | 2 heavy + 2 light chains, disulphide bonds; variable region binds antigen, Fc for effector functions; IgG most, crosses placenta; IgA secretory (milk); IgM pentamer, first response, IgM in newborn = intrauterine infection; IgD B-cell receptor; IgE allergy, worms; ELISA: enzyme + substrate → colour (OD); indirect detects antibody (HIV), sandwich detects antigen (HBsAg); above cut-off = reactive; confirm positives; window period |

**Haem breakdown in one line**

```text
RBC → Hb → haem → (haem oxygenase) biliverdin → (reductase) bilirubin + albumin → liver:
glucuronide (conjugated) → bile → gut bacteria → urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool) / urobilin (urine)
```

**Nursing links to quote**: fluoride tube for glucose; prepare correctly for OGTT and lipid profile; avoid haemolysis (falsely high K⁺, LDH, AST); record time of chest pain for troponin; PSA before rectal examination; ABG — Allen test, heparinised syringe, no air bubbles, pressure 5 minutes; fresh, light-protected urine for bile pigments; phototherapy care in neonatal jaundice; counselling and confidentiality in HIV testing; recognise hypoglycaemia and Kussmaul breathing.

**Exam pattern reminder**: Section A Applied Biochemistry = 4 MCQs (4) + 3 short (15) + 3 very short (6) = 25 marks, no essay, no choice. Applied Nutrition and Dietetics is Section B (50 marks) of the same 3-hour paper.

questions.answer:
1. Normal values (venous plasma, about): fasting 70–100 mg/dL; 2 h after a meal below 140 mg/dL. Blood glucose is kept steady because the brain depends on glucose.
2. Renal threshold about 180 mg/dL: above it, filtered glucose is not fully reabsorbed and appears in urine (glycosuria).
3. Insulin (β cells of islets) — the only hormone that lowers blood glucose: increases glucose entry into muscle and fat (GLUT-4), glycogenesis, fat synthesis; decreases gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
4. Glucagon (α cells) raises glucose: liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
5. Adrenaline: rapid rise in stress through glycogenolysis in liver and muscle.
6. Cortisol: raises glucose by gluconeogenesis and by reducing tissue uptake.
7. Growth hormone and thyroxine: anti-insulin effects; thyroxine increases absorption and glycogenolysis.
8. Role of liver: stores glucose as glycogen after meals and releases it in fasting (glycogenolysis first, gluconeogenesis later) — the glucose buffer.
9. Role of muscle and adipose tissue: take up glucose under insulin. Role of kidney: excretes glucose above threshold; gluconeogenesis in prolonged fasting.
10. Flow chart: after a meal glucose ↑ → insulin ↑ → glucose into cells → glucose ↓; in fasting glucose ↓ → glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline ↑ → liver releases glucose → glucose ↑.
11. Nursing: check glucose in fluoride tubes or by glucometer; watch for hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia in patients on insulin or steroids.
questions.question: Describe the regulation of blood glucose. Add a note on the normal values of blood glucose and the renal threshold.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a test of the body's ability to handle a standard glucose load; glucose measured fasting and at fixed times after drinking glucose.
2. Indications: borderline fasting/random glucose, glycosuria without symptoms (to rule out renal glycosuria), gestational diabetes screening, high-risk persons (family history, obesity, large baby), unexplained neuropathy or retinopathy.
3. Preparation: normal diet with adequate carbohydrate for 3 days; overnight fast of 8–14 h (water allowed); no smoking, tea or exercise on the test morning; note drugs that affect glucose.
4. Fasting blood (fluoride tube) and urine samples taken.
5. 75 g anhydrous glucose in about 250–300 mL water drunk within 5 minutes (children 1.75 g/kg, maximum 75 g); time noted.
6. Blood and urine samples every 30 minutes for 2 hours (or at least at 2 h); samples labelled with time; vomiting spoils the test.
7. Interpretation (about): normal — fasting below 100, 2 h below 140 mg/dL; impaired glucose tolerance — 2 h 140–199; diabetes — fasting ≥126 or 2 h ≥200 mg/dL.
8. Normal curve: peak within 30–60 min below renal threshold, back to fasting level by 2 h, no glycosuria.
9. Diabetic curve: high fasting, high peak, high at 2 h, glycosuria.
10. Lag (alimentary) curve: sharp early peak above 180 with brief glycosuria, normal by 2 h — after gastrectomy, hyperthyroidism.
11. Flat curve: very small rise — malabsorption, hypothyroidism, Addison's disease. Renal glycosuria: normal blood curve with glucose in urine.
12. Draw the curves (time on x-axis, glucose on y-axis, dotted line at 180 mg/dL).
questions.question: What is the oral glucose tolerance test? Write its indications, procedure and interpretation, with the types of GTT curve.

questions.answer: Table points: (1) Cause — type 1 autoimmune destruction of β cells (absolute insulin deficiency); type 2 insulin resistance with relative deficiency. (2) Age — type 1 children/young adults; type 2 adults. (3) Build — type 1 thin; type 2 often obese. (4) Onset — sudden vs gradual. (5) Ketoacidosis — common in type 1, uncommon in type 2 (hyperosmolar state more typical). (6) Family history stronger in type 2. (7) Treatment — type 1 always insulin; type 2 diet, exercise, oral drugs, insulin later in some. (8) Both cause long-term micro- and macrovascular complications.
questions.question: Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

questions.answer:
1. Symptoms: polyuria — glucose above renal threshold causes osmotic diuresis; polydipsia — water loss; polyphagia — cells starved of glucose; weight loss — fat and protein breakdown; infections and slow healing.
2. Acute complications: diabetic ketoacidosis (ketone bodies, metabolic acidosis, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath); hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; hypoglycaemia from treatment.
3. Chronic microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy (microalbuminuria → kidney failure), neuropathy.
4. Chronic macrovascular: coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, diabetic foot and gangrene.
5. Nursing: foot care, glucose monitoring, yearly eye and urine albumin checks.
questions.question: Write the complications of diabetes mellitus and the biochemical basis of its symptoms.

questions.answer:
1. Mini GTT: only fasting and 2-hour blood (and urine) samples after 75 g glucose; quick, cheap, widely used for screening.
2. Extended GTT: samples continued every 30–60 min up to 4–6 hours; used for suspected reactive hypoglycaemia, where glucose falls 3–5 h after the load.
3. Glucose challenge test (GCT): 50 g glucose at any time without fasting, one sample at 1 h; screening for gestational diabetes; a raised value (commonly ≥140 mg/dL) is followed by full OGTT.
4. Intravenous GTT: glucose given into a vein and blood sampled at intervals; used when oral absorption is unreliable — malabsorption, after gastric surgery, vomiting.
5. India's national guideline for gestational diabetes uses a single-step 75 g oral test; check the current guideline.
questions.question: Write short notes on the variants of the glucose tolerance test: mini GTT, extended GTT, GCT and IV GTT.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: blood glucose low enough to cause symptoms; plasma glucose below about 70 mg/dL is treated as hypoglycaemia; Whipple's triad — symptoms, low measured glucose, relief when glucose is raised.
2. Causes: excess insulin or sulphonylurea, missed meal, unusual exercise (commonest); alcohol; insulinoma; liver failure; adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism; starvation; inborn errors (glycogen storage disease, galactosaemia, fructose intolerance); newborns of diabetic mothers, preterm babies; reactive hypoglycaemia after gastric surgery.
3. Features: sweating, tremor, palpitation, hunger, anxiety; then confusion, abnormal behaviour, fits, coma.
4. Nursing: check glucose, give quick-acting sugar to a conscious patient as per protocol, recheck, find the cause.
questions.question: Define hypoglycaemia. List its causes and clinical features.

questions.answer:
1. Mouth: salivary amylase (ptyalin) breaks starch to dextrins and maltose; stopped by stomach acid.
2. Stomach: no carbohydrate enzyme of its own.
3. Duodenum: pancreatic amylase converts starch and dextrins to maltose, isomaltose and limit dextrins.
4. Brush border: maltase, isomaltase, sucrase and lactase give glucose, fructose and galactose.
5. Cellulose is not digested — acts as dietary fibre.
6. Absorption: glucose and galactose by sodium-linked active transport (SGLT-1); fructose by facilitated diffusion (GLUT-5); all leave by GLUT-2 into portal blood to the liver.
7. Disorder: lactase deficiency → lactose intolerance (bloating, diarrhoea). Nursing: glucose–sodium co-transport is the basis of ORS.
questions.question: Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates.

questions.answer: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) is haemoglobin A with glucose attached non-enzymatically. Because RBCs live about 120 days, it reflects the average blood glucose of the previous 2–3 months; about 6.5% or above supports diabetes.
questions.question: Define HbA1c and state its significance.

questions.answer: The blood glucose level above which the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose, so glucose appears in urine — about 180 mg/dL.
questions.question: What is the renal threshold for glucose?

questions.answer: A GTT curve with a sharp early peak above the renal threshold (with brief glycosuria) at 30–60 minutes that returns to normal by 2 hours; seen after gastrectomy and in hyperthyroidism.
questions.question: What is a lag curve in the GTT?

questions.answer: Glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone and thyroxine (insulin is the only hormone that lowers it).
questions.question: Name the hormones that raise blood glucose.

questions.answer: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate (or lactate without oxygen) in the cytoplasm of all cells; it gives a net 2 ATP per glucose.
questions.question: What is glycolysis? Give its net ATP yield.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group at one end; usually an even number of carbons; found mostly as esters in fats.
2. By chain length: short (up to 6 C, butyric), medium (8–12 C, caprylic), long (14 C and more, palmitic, stearic).
3. By saturation: saturated (palmitic, stearic), MUFA (oleic, ω-9), PUFA (linoleic ω-6, α-linolenic ω-3, arachidonic ω-6, EPA, DHA).
4. By need: essential (linoleic, α-linolenic; arachidonic if linoleic is lacking), non-essential (palmitic, oleic).
5. By shape: cis (natural) and trans (from partial hydrogenation).
6. MUFA (olive, groundnut, mustard, rice-bran oil): lower LDL, keep HDL — heart-protective.
7. PUFA: ω-6 lowers LDL; ω-3 (fish, flaxseed) lowers triglycerides, reduces clotting and inflammation; DHA for foetal brain and retina.
8. Essential fatty acids: needed for membranes, skin and eicosanoids (prostaglandins, leukotrienes); deficiency → phrynoderma, poor growth, fatty liver.
9. Trans fatty acids (vanaspati, bakery, re-used frying oil): raise LDL and lower HDL — increase heart disease; India's food regulator limits them.
10. Saturated fats raise LDL when eaten in excess.
11. Nursing: diet teaching — mix of oils, avoid vanaspati and re-used oil, include ω-3 sources.
questions.question: Define fatty acids and classify them with examples. Explain the clinical significance of MUFA, PUFA, essential fatty acids and trans fatty acids.

questions.answer:
1. Lipoproteins carry insoluble lipids in plasma: core of triacylglycerol and cholesterol esters, shell of phospholipid, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins.
2. Chylomicrons: made in intestine; carry dietary fat to tissues; lowest density, largest.
3. VLDL: made in liver; carry endogenous triacylglycerol to tissues.
4. IDL: formed from VLDL; becomes LDL.
5. LDL: richest in cholesterol; carries cholesterol to tissues; excess enters artery walls — 'bad cholesterol'.
6. HDL: reverse cholesterol transport from tissues to liver — 'good cholesterol'; highest density.
7. Electrophoresis: HDL = α, LDL = β, VLDL = pre-β; chylomicrons at origin. Lp(a) — inherited risk factor.
8. Lipid profile preparation: 10–12 h fast if the lab asks; no alcohol or fatty meal the day before.
9. Desirable (about): total cholesterol below 200 mg/dL; LDL below 100; HDL above 40 (men) / 50 (women); TG below 150; VLDL about TG ÷ 5.
10. Friedewald formula: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5 (valid if TG below about 400).
11. Significance: high LDL and low HDL predict atherosclerosis and coronary disease.
questions.question: What are lipoproteins? Give the types and functions of lipoproteins. Add a note on the lipid profile and its normal values.

questions.answer:
1. Ketone bodies are compounds made in liver mitochondria from excess acetyl-CoA.
2. Types: acetoacetate (primary), β-hydroxybutyrate (formed by reduction of acetoacetate), acetone (volatile, breathed out — fruity breath).
3. Normal fuel for heart, skeletal muscle and kidney; brain uses them in prolonged starvation; liver cannot use them.
4. Ketosis: starvation, prolonged vomiting, uncontrolled diabetes, very low-carbohydrate diet, alcohol excess.
5. Ketoacidosis: acids use up bicarbonate → high anion gap metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, coma (DKA).
6. Detection: Rothera's test/dipstick detects acetoacetate and acetone, not β-hydroxybutyrate.
questions.question: What are ketone bodies? Write their types and significance.

questions.answer:
1. Mouth/stomach: lingual and gastric lipase — minor role (more in infants).
2. Duodenum: bile salts emulsify fat into fine droplets.
3. Pancreatic lipase with colipase: triacylglycerol → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 fatty acids; cholesterol esterase and phospholipase A2 act on cholesterol esters and phospholipids.
4. Products with bile salts form micelles that reach the brush border.
5. In mucosal cells long-chain fatty acids are re-esterified and packed with apo B-48 into chylomicrons → lacteals → thoracic duct → blood.
6. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids go directly into portal blood.
7. Bile salts reabsorbed in ileum (enterohepatic circulation).
8. Disorder: lack of bile or lipase → steatorrhoea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, K.
questions.question: Describe the digestion and absorption of lipids.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: disease of large and medium arteries with lipid-rich plaques in the intima, narrowing the lumen.
2. Risk factors: high LDL, low HDL, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, inactivity, family history, age, male sex.
3. Process: endothelial injury → LDL enters intima and is oxidised → macrophages take it up → foam cells → fatty streak → smooth muscle and collagen → fibrous plaque → calcification; rupture → thrombus.
4. Results: angina, myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, aneurysm.
5. Prevention: diet low in saturated and trans fat, exercise, weight control, stop smoking, control BP, sugar and lipids.
questions.question: Write short notes on atherosclerosis.

questions.answer:
1. Bile acids/bile salts (cholic, chenodeoxycholic) — emulsify fats; main route of cholesterol removal.
2. Glucocorticoids (cortisol) — glucose metabolism, stress response.
3. Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) — sodium and water retention.
4. Sex hormones: progesterone, testosterone, oestrogens — reproduction.
5. Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) — formed from 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin by sunlight; calcium absorption.
6. Cholesterol itself is a part of cell membranes and myelin.
questions.question: Name the compounds formed from cholesterol and give their functions.

questions.answer:
1. Disorders: obesity, fatty liver, dyslipidaemias (hyperlipoproteinaemias types I–V, familial hypercholesterolaemia), ketosis/ketoacidosis, lipid storage diseases (Tay-Sachs, Gaucher's, Niemann-Pick), steatorrhoea, atherosclerosis, surfactant deficiency in preterm babies.
2. Fatty liver: excess fat in liver cells when fat is made or brought in faster than it is exported as VLDL.
3. Causes: alcohol, obesity, diabetes, protein deficiency (kwashiorkor), lack of lipotropic factors (choline, methionine), some toxins.
4. Effects: enlarged liver, raised liver enzymes; may progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis.
5. Prevention: avoid alcohol, weight control, adequate protein.
questions.question: List the disorders of lipid metabolism. Explain fatty liver.

questions.answer: Linoleic acid (ω-6) and α-linolenic acid (ω-3); arachidonic acid becomes essential when linoleic acid is lacking.
questions.question: Name the essential fatty acids.

questions.answer: Unsaturated fatty acids with a trans double bond, formed mainly by partial hydrogenation (vanaspati, bakery foods). They raise LDL and lower HDL, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease.
questions.question: What are trans fatty acids? Why are they harmful?

questions.answer: HDL carries excess cholesterol from tissues and artery walls back to the liver for removal (reverse cholesterol transport), so high HDL protects against atherosclerosis.
questions.question: Why is HDL called 'good cholesterol'?

questions.answer: LDL cholesterol = Total cholesterol − HDL cholesterol − (Triglycerides ÷ 5), all in mg/dL; valid when triglycerides are below about 400 mg/dL.
questions.question: Write the Friedewald formula.

questions.answer:
1. Amino acids are building blocks of proteins with an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain; 20 are used in human proteins.
2. Essential (from diet): valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine.
3. Semi-essential: arginine and histidine (needed during growth). Memory: PVT TIM HALL.
4. Non-essential: glycine, alanine, serine, aspartate, glutamate, asparagine, glutamine, proline, tyrosine, cysteine.
5. Purely ketogenic: leucine, lysine.
6. Ketogenic and glucogenic: isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan.
7. Purely glucogenic: the rest — alanine, glycine, serine, glutamate, aspartate, methionine, valine, histidine, arginine.
8. Compounds: glycine → haem, creatine, glutathione, purines, glycocholic acid; tyrosine → dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline, thyroxine, melanin; tryptophan → serotonin, melatonin, niacin; histidine → histamine; arginine → nitric oxide, creatine, urea; methionine → S-adenosylmethionine, cysteine; cysteine → taurine; glutamate → GABA.
9. Nutrition point: cereal (low lysine) + pulse (low methionine) together improve protein quality.
questions.question: Classify amino acids on the basis of nutritional requirement and metabolic fate with examples. Write the biologically important compounds formed from amino acids.

questions.answer:
1. Plasma proteins: albumin, globulins (α1, α2, β, γ) and fibrinogen; most made in the liver, γ-globulins by plasma cells.
2. Normal (about): total protein 6–8 g/dL; albumin 3.5–5.0; globulin 2–3.5 g/dL; A:G ratio above 1 (about 1.5–2 : 1); fibrinogen 200–400 mg/dL.
3. Albumin: maintains oncotic pressure (about 80%); transports bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium, hormones, drugs; buffer; nutrition.
4. α1: α1-antitrypsin (protects lungs). α2: haptoglobin (binds free Hb), ceruloplasmin (copper). β: transferrin (iron), LDL, complement. γ: immunoglobulins (defence).
5. Fibrinogen and prothrombin: clotting. Acute phase proteins such as CRP rise in inflammation.
6. Low albumin → oedema and ascites.
7. Hypoproteinaemia causes: low intake (malnutrition, kwashiorkor); malabsorption; low synthesis (liver disease); increased loss (nephrotic syndrome, burns, protein-losing enteropathy, haemorrhage); increased breakdown (fever, sepsis, cancer); dilution (over-hydration, pregnancy).
8. Nursing: daily weight, oedema check, protein-rich diet as advised.
questions.question: What are plasma proteins? Write their types, functions and normal values. Add the causes of hypoproteinaemia.

questions.answer:
1. Phenylketonuria: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; phenylalanine accumulates → intellectual disability, fits, mousy odour, fair skin; newborn screening (Guthrie test); lifelong low-phenylalanine diet.
2. Alkaptonuria: homogentisate oxidase deficiency; urine turns black on standing; ochronosis; arthritis later.
3. Albinism: tyrosinase deficiency; no melanin — white hair, pale skin, photophobia, poor vision, skin cancer risk; sun protection.
4. Tyrosinaemia type I: fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency; liver and kidney damage.
5. Hartnup disease (tryptophan transport): pellagra-like rash.
questions.question: Write a note on inborn errors of aromatic amino acid metabolism.

questions.answer:
1. Stomach: HCl denatures protein and converts pepsinogen to pepsin; pepsin gives large peptides; rennin clots milk in infants.
2. Pancreas: trypsinogen activated to trypsin by enteropeptidase; trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase; endopeptidases cut inside the chain, carboxypeptidase from the end.
3. Brush border: aminopeptidases, dipeptidases, tripeptidases release free amino acids.
4. Enzymes released as inactive zymogens to protect the gland.
5. Absorption: sodium-dependent active transport of amino acids; di- and tripeptides also absorbed; γ-glutamyl cycle minor route; to liver by portal vein.
6. Newborns absorb some intact antibodies from colostrum.
questions.question: Describe the digestion and absorption of proteins.

questions.answer:
1. Normal urine protein is below about 150 mg/day; microalbuminuria 30–300 mg/day is early kidney damage.
2. Physiological/functional: exercise, fever, cold, stress, orthostatic proteinuria, pregnancy.
3. Glomerular: nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, hypertension, pre-eclampsia, SLE.
4. Tubular: tubular damage by heavy metals, drugs, pyelonephritis.
5. Overflow: Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria.
6. Post-renal: urinary tract infection, stones, tumours.
7. Tests: dipstick, heat and acetic acid, sulphosalicylic acid, 24-hour urine protein.
questions.question: Write the causes of proteinuria.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: charged particles move in an electric field; at pH 8.6 serum proteins are negatively charged and move towards the anode at speeds depending on charge, size and shape.
2. Method: serum applied on cellulose acetate or agarose, current passed, strip stained, bands read by densitometer.
3. Normal: albumin (fastest, tall), α1, α2, β, γ (broad, near origin).
4. Nephrotic syndrome: albumin ↓↓, α2 ↑.
5. Cirrhosis: albumin ↓, polyclonal γ ↑ with β–γ bridging.
6. Multiple myeloma: narrow M band in γ region.
7. Chronic infection: broad γ ↑. Acute inflammation: α1, α2 ↑. α1-antitrypsin deficiency: α1 band absent.
questions.question: Explain the principle of electrophoresis. Describe the normal and abnormal electrophoretic patterns of serum proteins.

questions.answer:
1. Removes toxic ammonia as urea; occurs only in the liver, partly in mitochondria and partly in cytoplasm.
2. Steps: NH3 + CO2 → carbamoyl phosphate (CPS-I) → with ornithine forms citrulline (OTC) → with aspartate forms argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate → arginase splits arginine into urea and ornithine.
3. Uses 3 ATP per urea; urea goes by blood to kidney.
4. Ammonia reaches liver as glutamine and alanine.
5. Clinical: liver failure or urea cycle enzyme defects → hyperammonaemia (vomiting, flapping tremor, coma — hepatic encephalopathy); blood urea rises in kidney failure.
questions.question: Write about the urea cycle and its clinical importance.

questions.answer: Valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and lysine; arginine and histidine are semi-essential (memory: PVT TIM HALL).
questions.question: Name the essential amino acids.

questions.answer: An inborn error due to deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase; phenylalanine and phenylketones accumulate, causing intellectual disability and a mousy body odour. It is detected by newborn screening and treated with a low-phenylalanine diet.
questions.question: What is phenylketonuria?

questions.answer: Free immunoglobulin light chains in urine, seen in multiple myeloma; they precipitate at about 40–60 °C, redissolve near boiling and reappear on cooling.
questions.question: What is Bence Jones protein?

questions.answer: Leucine and lysine.
questions.question: Name two purely ketogenic amino acids.

questions.answer:
1. Isoenzymes: different molecular forms of the same enzyme that catalyse the same reaction but differ in structure and physical, chemical and immunological properties.
2. Properties: different amino acid composition/sub-units; electrophoretic mobility; tissue distribution (organ specificity); kinetic properties (Km); heat stability; response to inhibitors; immunological properties; sub-cellular location.
3. CK isoenzymes: BB (brain), MB (heart), MM (skeletal muscle).
4. LDH isoenzymes: LDH-1 to LDH-5; LDH-1 heart and RBC, LDH-5 liver and muscle.
5. Cardiac troponins I and T: rise about 3–6 h, peak 12–24 h, remain 7–14 days; most specific — marker of choice.
6. CK-MB: rises 3–6 h, peaks 12–24 h, normal in 2–3 days; useful for re-infarction.
7. AST: rises 6–8 h, peaks 24–48 h, normal in 4–6 days; not specific.
8. LDH: rises 12–24 h, peaks 2–3 days, normal by 8–14 days; LDH-1 > LDH-2 (flipped pattern).
9. Draw a time-course graph of the markers.
10. Nursing: record time of chest pain and of sampling; avoid haemolysis; report rising troponin.
questions.question: Define isoenzymes and write their properties. Describe the enzymes of diagnostic importance in myocardial infarction.

questions.answer:
1. ALT: mainly liver — most liver-specific; very high in acute viral hepatitis.
2. AST: liver, heart, muscle, RBC — less specific; AST : ALT more than 2 in alcoholic liver disease.
3. ALP: from bile canaliculi; marked rise in obstructive jaundice (gallstone, carcinoma head of pancreas); also bone disease.
4. GGT: rises in alcohol use, cholestasis, enzyme-inducing drugs; confirms that a raised ALP is from liver.
5. Patterns: hepatocellular — ALT/AST ↑↑; cholestatic — ALP/GGT ↑↑.
questions.question: Write the enzymes of diagnostic importance in liver diseases.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: different forms of the same enzyme catalysing the same reaction, differing in structure, electrophoretic mobility, tissue distribution and other properties.
2. CK is a dimer of M and B sub-units: CK-BB (brain), CK-MB (heart — raised in MI), CK-MM (skeletal muscle — raised in muscle injury, dystrophy, IM injections).
3. LDH is a tetramer of H and M sub-units: LDH-1 (H4, heart, RBC), LDH-2 (heart, RBC; normally the largest), LDH-3 (lungs, spleen), LDH-4, LDH-5 (M4, liver, muscle).
4. MI: LDH-1 > LDH-2 (flipped). Liver disease: LDH-5 ↑. Haemolysis raises LDH falsely.
questions.question: Define isoenzymes. Write a note on the isoenzymes of CK and LDH.

questions.answer:
1. Bone — ALP (from osteoblasts): raised in rickets, osteomalacia, Paget's disease (very high), osteoblastic bone secondaries, healing fractures, hyperparathyroidism; normally high in children and pregnancy.
2. Muscle — CK (MM): very high in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (also in carriers), polymyositis, crush injury, rhabdomyolysis; aldolase also raised.
3. Prostate — PSA: main marker for screening and follow-up; above about 4 ng/mL needs work-up; also raised in BPH, prostatitis, after rectal examination or catheterisation.
4. Prostatic ACP (tartrate-labile): raised when cancer spreads beyond the capsule, especially to bone.
questions.question: Write about the enzymes of diagnostic importance in bone diseases, muscle diseases and prostate cancer.

questions.answer:
1. Functional plasma enzymes act in plasma and are normally present in high amounts — clotting factors, lipoprotein lipase.
2. Non-functional enzymes work inside cells; only small amounts leak into plasma — ALT, AST, CK, LDH, ALP, GGT, amylase.
3. Cell damage or increased production raises their plasma level.
4. The enzyme (and isoenzyme) points to the organ damaged; the time pattern shows when damage occurred and how much.
5. Examples: troponin/CK-MB in MI, ALT in hepatitis, amylase/lipase in pancreatitis, ALP in bone and biliary disease.
questions.question: What are functional and non-functional plasma enzymes? Why are plasma enzymes useful in diagnosis?

questions.answer: Normally LDH-2 is higher than LDH-1 in serum; after myocardial infarction LDH-1 (from heart muscle) rises above LDH-2 — the flipped pattern.
questions.question: What is the 'flipped LDH pattern'?

questions.answer: Cardiac troponin (I or T), because cardiac troponins differ in structure from skeletal muscle troponins and are released only when heart muscle is damaged; they stay raised for 7–14 days.
questions.question: Which cardiac marker is the most specific for myocardial infarction? Why?

questions.answer: Prostate-specific antigen, a protease made by prostate gland cells. It is raised in prostate cancer, and also in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis and after rectal examination or catheterisation.
questions.question: What is PSA? When is it raised?

questions.answer: RBCs contain LDH, AST, acid phosphatase and potassium; haemolysis releases them and gives falsely high values.
questions.question: Why should haemolysis be avoided in samples for enzyme tests?

questions.answer:
1. pH = negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration; normal blood pH about 7.35–7.45.
2. Three lines of defence: buffers (seconds), lungs (minutes), kidneys (hours to days).
3. Bicarbonate buffer: H2CO3/HCO3⁻, main buffer of blood; acid added → H2CO3 → CO2 breathed out.
4. Phosphate buffer (cells, urine), protein buffer, haemoglobin buffer (H⁺ from CO2 transport).
5. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3⁻]/(0.03 × pCO2); ratio 20 : 1 gives pH 7.4.
6. Lungs: acidosis stimulates respiratory centre → deep fast breathing → CO2 blown off; alkalosis → slow breathing → CO2 retained.
7. Kidneys: reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate; excretion of H⁺ as titratable acid with phosphate; excretion of NH4⁺ (ammonia from glutamine) — main response in chronic acidosis; each H⁺ excreted adds a new HCO3⁻ to blood.
8. Urine pH ranges about 4.5–8.
9. Nursing: count respiratory rate and depth; ABG sampling care.
questions.question: Define pH and give its normal value in blood. Explain the regulation of blood pH by blood buffers, the lungs and the kidneys.

questions.answer:
1. Metabolic acidosis: primary fall in HCO3⁻ with low pH — DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea, poisoning.
2. Metabolic alkalosis: primary rise in HCO3⁻ with high pH — vomiting, nasogastric aspiration, diuretics, hypokalaemia, excess alkali.
3. Respiratory acidosis: primary rise in PaCO2 with low pH — COPD, severe asthma, respiratory depression by drugs, neuromuscular weakness.
4. Respiratory alkalosis: primary fall in PaCO2 with high pH — hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, fever), high altitude, early salicylate poisoning.
5. Compensation: lungs for metabolic, kidneys for respiratory disorders. ROME — Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.
questions.question: Write the types, definitions and causes of acid–base disorders.

questions.answer:
1. A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt that resists change in pH.
2. Blood buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, protein and haemoglobin.
3. Bicarbonate buffer: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO3⁻ (carbonic anhydrase).
4. Strong acid added: HCl + NaHCO3 → NaCl + H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O, CO2 breathed out.
5. Strong base added: NaOH + H2CO3 → NaHCO3 + H2O; extra bicarbonate excreted by kidney.
6. pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3⁻]/[H2CO3]; ratio 20 : 1 gives 7.4; it is the most important blood buffer because both parts are regulated (lungs and kidneys).
questions.question: What are blood buffers? Explain the bicarbonate buffer system.

questions.answer:
1. Tubular cells use carbonic anhydrase to make H⁺ and HCO3⁻ from CO2 and water.
2. Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate (proximal tubule) — bicarbonate saved.
3. Excretion of titratable acid: H⁺ buffered by phosphate in tubular fluid; new HCO3⁻ returned to blood.
4. Excretion of ammonium: ammonia made from glutamine traps H⁺ as NH4⁺ — main adaptation in chronic acidosis.
5. Urine pH can fall to about 4.5 or rise to about 8.
6. Slow (hours to days) but the only route to remove fixed acids.
questions.question: Explain the renal regulation of acid–base balance.

questions.answer:
1. Normal (about): pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO2 35–45 mmHg; HCO3⁻ 22–26 mmol/L; PaO2 80–100 mmHg; SaO2 95–100%; base excess −2 to +2.
2. Step 1: pH — acidaemia or alkalaemia.
3. Step 2: PaCO2 — respiratory cause if it moves opposite to pH.
4. Step 3: HCO3⁻ — metabolic cause if it moves with pH.
5. Step 4: compensation — partial if pH still abnormal, full if pH normal.
6. Step 5: oxygenation; step 6: anion gap in metabolic acidosis.
7. Example: pH 7.25, PaCO2 30, HCO3⁻ 14 = partly compensated metabolic acidosis.
questions.question: Write the normal ABG values and the steps to interpret an ABG report.

questions.answer: pH is the negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration; normal blood pH is about 7.35–7.45.
questions.question: Define pH and give the normal blood pH.

questions.answer: Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻); normal about 8–16 mmol/L. It is raised in metabolic acidosis due to added acids such as ketones or lactate.
questions.question: What is the anion gap?

questions.answer: Prolonged vomiting and continuous nasogastric aspiration (loss of stomach acid); also diuretics and hypokalaemia.
questions.question: Name two causes of metabolic alkalosis.

questions.answer: Deep, rapid breathing seen in metabolic acidosis (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis); the lungs blow off CO2 to compensate for the acidosis.
questions.question: What is Kussmaul breathing?

questions.answer:
1. Old RBCs (about 120 days) broken down in reticuloendothelial cells (spleen); haemoglobin → globin + haem.
2. Haem oxygenase: haem → biliverdin + iron + CO; biliverdin reductase: biliverdin → bilirubin (unconjugated).
3. Unconjugated bilirubin carried on albumin to liver; conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronyl transferase → bilirubin diglucuronide.
4. Secreted into bile → intestine → bacteria form urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool); some reabsorbed, small part excreted as urine urobilinogen/urobilin.
5. Normal serum bilirubin about 0.2–1.2 mg/dL; direct up to 0.3; jaundice visible above about 2–3 mg/dL.
6. Pre-hepatic (haemolytic): unconjugated ↑, indirect van den Bergh, urine bilirubin absent, urobilinogen ↑, dark stool.
7. Hepatic: both ↑, biphasic, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen variable, ALT/AST ↑↑.
8. Post-hepatic (obstructive): conjugated ↑, direct reaction, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen absent, bile salts present, clay-coloured stool, ALP/GGT ↑↑, itching.
9. Nursing: observe sclera, urine and stool; phototherapy care in newborns.
questions.question: Describe the haem degradation pathway. Classify jaundice and give the laboratory findings in each type.

questions.answer: Table: (1) Serum unconjugated bilirubin — haemolytic ↑↑, hepatic ↑, obstructive normal/slight ↑. (2) Conjugated — normal, ↑, ↑↑. (3) van den Bergh — indirect, biphasic, direct. (4) Urine bilirubin — absent, present, present. (5) Urine urobilinogen — ↑↑, variable, absent. (6) Bile salts in urine — absent, may be present, present. (7) Stool — dark, normal/pale, clay-coloured. (8) Enzymes — normal; ALT/AST ↑↑; ALP/GGT ↑↑.
questions.question: Differentiate between the types of jaundice based on blood and urine findings.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: bilirubin reacts with diazotised sulphanilic acid (diazo reagent) to form purple azobilirubin.
2. Direct reaction: colour appears at once in watery solution — conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin — obstructive jaundice.
3. Indirect reaction: colour appears only after adding alcohol (methanol), which dissolves unconjugated bilirubin — haemolytic jaundice.
4. Biphasic: some colour at once, more after alcohol — hepatic jaundice.
5. Modern analysers report total and direct bilirubin by the same principle; indirect = total − direct.
questions.question: Explain the van den Bergh test.

questions.answer:
1. Blood urea about 15–40 mg/dL (BUN 7–20).
2. Serum creatinine about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL — better index of GFR.
3. Serum uric acid about 3.5–7 mg/dL (men), 2.5–6 (women).
4. Electrolytes: Na⁺ 135–145, K⁺ 3.5–5.0, Cl⁻ about 96–106, HCO3⁻ 22–26 mmol/L.
5. GFR about 120 mL/min; creatinine clearance about 90–130 mL/min (U × V / P); eGFR above 90 normal.
6. Urine: volume 1–2 L/day, specific gravity 1.003–1.030, pH about 4.5–8, protein below 150 mg/day, no glucose or ketones.
7. Values are approximate; follow the lab's range.
questions.question: Write the biochemical parameters and normal values of renal function tests.

questions.answer:
1. Serum bilirubin total about 0.2–1.2 mg/dL; direct up to 0.3.
2. ALT about 7–40 U/L and AST about 8–40 U/L (ranges vary widely between labs).
3. ALP about 40–130 U/L in adults (higher in children and pregnancy); GGT about 10–50 U/L.
4. Total protein 6–8 g/dL; albumin 3.5–5 g/dL; globulin 2–3.5 g/dL; A:G above 1.
5. Prothrombin time about 11–14 s; INR about 1 — prolonged in liver failure.
6. Urine bilirubin absent, urobilinogen in trace amounts.
7. Patterns: hepatocellular (ALT/AST ↑↑), cholestatic (ALP/GGT ↑↑), chronic (albumin ↓, PT ↑).
questions.question: Write the parameters and normal values of liver function tests.

questions.answer:
1. TSH about 0.4–4.5 mIU/L — best single screening test.
2. Total T4 about 5–12 µg/dL; free T4 about 0.8–1.8 ng/dL; total T3 about 80–200 ng/dL; free T3 about 2.3–4.2 pg/mL.
3. Anti-TPO antibodies raised in autoimmune thyroiditis.
4. Primary hypothyroidism: TSH ↑, T4 ↓. Subclinical: TSH ↑, T4 normal.
5. Primary hyperthyroidism: TSH ↓, T4/T3 ↑. Secondary hypothyroidism: TSH low or normal, T4 ↓.
6. Newborn screening prevents cretinism; pregnancy has its own ranges.
questions.question: Write the thyroid function tests with normal values and interpretation.

questions.answer: Mild unconjugated jaundice appearing after 24 hours (days 2–3) and fading within 1–2 weeks, due to high RBC breakdown and an immature liver conjugating enzyme.
questions.question: What is physiological jaundice of the newborn?

questions.answer: Bile pigments — Fouchet's test; bile salts — Hay's sulphur test; urobilinogen — Ehrlich's test.
questions.question: Name the urine tests for bile pigments, bile salts and urobilinogen.

questions.answer: It is insoluble in water and is carried tightly bound to albumin, so it is not filtered by the glomerulus.
questions.question: Why is unconjugated bilirubin not found in urine?

questions.answer: Blood urea about 15–40 mg/dL; serum creatinine about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL (values vary with the lab).
questions.question: Give the normal values of blood urea and serum creatinine.

questions.answer:
1. Immunoglobulins are glycoproteins (γ-globulins) made by plasma cells.
2. Y-shaped monomer: 2 identical heavy chains and 2 identical light chains (κ or λ), joined by disulphide bonds.
3. Variable region at the tips of the arms forms the antigen-binding site (hypervariable regions); constant region decides effector function.
4. Hinge region gives flexibility; Fab binds antigen (2 sites); Fc binds complement, phagocytes, mast cells, placenta.
5. Papain gives 2 Fab + 1 Fc; pepsin gives F(ab')2.
6. IgG: monomer, 75–80%, crosses placenta, secondary response, longest half-life.
7. IgA: dimer in secretions, colostrum, milk — mucosal immunity.
8. IgM: pentamer, largest, first in primary response, best complement activator, anti-A/anti-B.
9. IgD: B-cell surface receptor. IgE: allergy and worm infections; binds mast cells.
10. Draw the labelled Y diagram.
questions.question: Describe the structure of an immunoglobulin with a diagram. Write the classes of immunoglobulins and their functions.

questions.answer:
1. Glycoprotein, Y-shaped, made by plasma cells.
2. Two heavy chains (class-specific: γ, α, μ, δ, ε) and two light chains (κ or λ).
3. Chains linked by inter- and intra-chain disulphide bonds.
4. Variable region (N-terminal ends) — antigen-binding site with hypervariable regions; constant region — effector functions.
5. Hinge region between the arms and stem gives flexibility.
6. Fab (antigen binding, 2 per monomer) and Fc (complement activation, binding to cells, placental transfer).
7. Papain → 2 Fab + Fc; pepsin → F(ab')2. Diagram expected.
questions.question: Describe the structure of immunoglobulin.

questions.answer:
1. IgG: most abundant (75–80%), monomer, crosses placenta, secondary response, neutralises toxins, opsonises.
2. IgA: secretory dimer in colostrum, milk, saliva, tears and mucosa — local immunity.
3. IgM: pentamer, largest, first antibody in the primary response, activates complement; IgM in a newborn means intrauterine infection.
4. IgD: on B-cell surface, acts as antigen receptor.
5. IgE: lowest level; binds mast cells and basophils; allergy and defence against worms.
questions.question: Write the classes of immunoglobulins with their functions.

questions.answer:
1. ELISA = enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
2. Principle: antigen–antibody reaction on a solid surface; one reactant linked to an enzyme (peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase); substrate gives a coloured product; colour (optical density) proportional to the amount present.
3. Types: direct; indirect (detects antibody — HIV, HCV antibody); sandwich (detects antigen — HBsAg, dengue NS1, hCG); competitive (less colour = more antigen).
4. Steps (indirect): coat antigen → add serum → wash → add enzyme-labelled anti-human Ig → wash → substrate → stop → read OD.
5. Interpretation: OD above cut-off = reactive; below = non-reactive; near cut-off = equivocal, repeat.
6. Screening test — confirm positives as per national strategy; window period gives false negatives.
questions.question: Explain the principle, types and interpretation of ELISA.

questions.answer:
1. IgG crossing the placenta gives the newborn passive immunity.
2. IgM in cord/newborn blood indicates congenital infection (rubella, toxoplasma, CMV).
3. IgM antibody indicates recent infection; IgG past infection or immunity.
4. Secretory IgA in breast milk protects the baby's gut.
5. Raised IgE in allergy and worm infection.
6. Monoclonal Ig (M band) and Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma; low Ig → repeated infections.
7. Immunoglobulin preparations give passive immunisation (rabies, tetanus, hepatitis B, anti-D).
questions.question: Write the clinical significance of immunoglobulins.

questions.answer: IgG — the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, giving the foetus and newborn passive immunity.
questions.question: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta?

questions.answer: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; used to screen for HIV antibodies and hepatitis B surface antigen (also dengue NS1, hCG, TSH).
questions.question: What does ELISA stand for? Give two uses.

questions.answer: The period after infection when the infection is present but antibodies have not yet reached a detectable level, so an antibody test such as ELISA can be falsely negative.
questions.question: What is the window period?

questions.answer: Secretory IgA; it protects the baby's gut and respiratory mucosa against infection.

# Unit 1: Carbohydrates, blood glucose and diabetes mellitus

INC Unit I (8 hours): digestion, absorption and metabolism of carbohydrates and related disorders; regulation of blood glucose; diabetes mellitus; investigations of diabetes (OGTT and its variants, HbA1c); hypoglycaemia. This is the heaviest unit of the course and the most common source of essay-type and short questions.

> **About laboratory values.** All normal values in these notes are approximate ("about"). Each laboratory sets its own reference range according to its method and machine, so always read a report against the range printed on it. Diagnostic cut-offs for diabetes are the widely used ADA/WHO figures; your teacher or hospital may use a slightly different guideline.

## 1.1 Carbohydrates in brief

Carbohydrates are aldehyde or ketone derivatives of polyhydroxy alcohols. They are the main fuel of the body, especially for the brain and red blood cells.

| Class | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monosaccharides | Single sugar unit | Glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose |
| Disaccharides | Two units | Sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose), maltose (glucose + glucose) |
| Oligosaccharides | 3–10 units | Raffinose |
| Polysaccharides | Many units | Starch and glycogen (storage), cellulose (dietary fibre), heparin, hyaluronic acid |

Glucose is the key sugar: it is the form in which carbohydrate travels in blood and is used by every cell.

## 1.2 Digestion of carbohydrates

```text
MOUTH      Salivary amylase (ptyalin) → starch → dextrins + some maltose
           (short contact time; stopped by stomach acid)
STOMACH    No carbohydrate-digesting enzyme of its own
DUODENUM   Pancreatic amylase → starch/dextrins → maltose, isomaltose,
           limit dextrins
SMALL      Brush-border enzymes:
INTESTINE    Maltase      maltose  → glucose + glucose
             Isomaltase   isomaltose → glucose
             Sucrase      sucrose  → glucose + fructose
             Lactase      lactose  → glucose + galactose
```

- Cellulose cannot be digested by humans (no enzyme to break its β-1,4 links). It stays as fibre, adds bulk to stool and helps prevent constipation.
- The end products of carbohydrate digestion are **monosaccharides**: glucose, fructose and galactose.

## 1.3 Absorption

| Sugar | Mechanism | Carrier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glucose, galactose | Secondary active transport, linked with sodium | SGLT-1 on the brush border |
| Fructose | Facilitated diffusion (no energy) | GLUT-5 |
| All three | Leave the cell into blood | GLUT-2 on the basal side |

The absorbed sugars travel by the **portal vein to the liver**, which takes up a large share after a meal.

**Nursing link: oral rehydration solution (ORS).** Glucose and sodium are absorbed together by SGLT-1, and water follows. This is why ORS containing both glucose and sodium works even in diarrhoea, when other absorption is disturbed.

## 1.4 Metabolism of glucose — overview

```text
                       Glycogen
              glycogenesis ↑   ↓ glycogenolysis
Dietary   →   GLUCOSE  ──glycolysis──→  Pyruvate ──→ Acetyl-CoA ──→ TCA cycle → CO2 + H2O + ATP
glucose        ↑   │                     │  (no O2)                  │
   gluconeogenesis │ HMP shunt           ↓                           ↓
 (lactate, amino   ↓                   Lactate                    Fatty acids (excess)
  acids, glycerol) NADPH + ribose
```

| Pathway | Where | What it does | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Glycolysis** | Cytoplasm of all cells | Glucose → 2 pyruvate (with O2) or 2 lactate (without O2) | Net 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; only pathway that gives energy without oxygen; RBCs depend on it (no mitochondria) |
| **Link reaction** | Mitochondria | Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA | Pyruvate dehydrogenase needs thiamine (vitamin B1) and other B vitamins |
| **TCA (citric acid / Krebs) cycle** | Mitochondria | Acetyl-CoA oxidised to CO2 | Final common pathway for carbohydrate, fat and protein; produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain |
| **Glycogenesis** | Liver, muscle | Glucose → glycogen | Stores glucose after meals; stimulated by insulin |
| **Glycogenolysis** | Liver, muscle | Glycogen → glucose | Liver glycogen keeps blood glucose up between meals; muscle glycogen is used only by muscle (muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase) |
| **Gluconeogenesis** | Liver (mainly), kidney | New glucose from non-carbohydrates: lactate, glycerol, glucogenic amino acids | Keeps blood glucose up during fasting and starvation; stimulated by glucagon and cortisol |
| **HMP shunt (pentose phosphate pathway)** | Liver, RBC, adipose, adrenal | Makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate | NADPH needed for fat synthesis and to protect RBCs from oxidation |

**Energy yield**: complete oxidation of one glucose gives about 30–32 ATP by current figures (older textbooks give 36–38). Anaerobic glycolysis gives only 2.

**Cori cycle**: lactate made by working muscle and RBCs goes to the liver, is changed back to glucose (gluconeogenesis) and returns to muscle.

## 1.5 Disorders of carbohydrate metabolism

| Disorder | Defect | Main features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lactose intolerance** | Low lactase in the gut wall | Bloating, cramps and diarrhoea after milk; common in adults; manage with less milk, curd |
| **Diabetes mellitus** | Lack of insulin or resistance to it | Hyperglycaemia (see 1.7) |
| **Galactosaemia** | Enzyme deficiency in galactose use (commonly galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase) | Infant vomits, fails to thrive, jaundice, cataract, liver damage, mental retardation; remove milk sugar from diet |
| **Hereditary fructose intolerance** | Aldolase B deficiency | Hypoglycaemia and vomiting after fruit/sucrose |
| **Glycogen storage diseases** | Enzymes of glycogen breakdown, e.g. glucose-6-phosphatase (von Gierke disease) | Large liver, fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis |
| **G6PD deficiency** | Low NADPH in RBCs | Haemolysis after oxidant drugs, infections or fava beans; neonatal jaundice |
| **Lactic acidosis** | Excess lactate (shock, hypoxia) | Metabolic acidosis (see Unit 5) |
| **Hypoglycaemia** | Low blood glucose | See 1.10 |

## 1.6 Regulation of blood glucose

Blood glucose is kept within a narrow range because the brain uses glucose almost exclusively under normal conditions.

**Approximate normal values (venous plasma)**

| Test | About |
| --- | --- |
| Fasting plasma glucose | 70–100 mg/dL |
| 2 hours after a meal (post-prandial) | below 140 mg/dL |
| Random | below about 140 mg/dL in a healthy person |

**Renal threshold for glucose**: about 180 mg/dL. Above this, the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose and glucose appears in urine (glycosuria).

**Hormones that act on blood glucose**

| Hormone | Source | Effect on blood glucose | How |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Insulin** | β cells of pancreatic islets | **Lowers** (the only hormone that lowers it) | ↑ glucose entry into muscle and fat (GLUT-4), ↑ glycogenesis, ↑ fat synthesis, ↓ gluconeogenesis, ↓ glycogenolysis |
| Glucagon | α cells of islets | Raises | ↑ glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver |
| Adrenaline | Adrenal medulla | Raises (quickly, in stress) | ↑ glycogenolysis in liver and muscle |
| Cortisol | Adrenal cortex | Raises | ↑ gluconeogenesis; ↓ glucose use in tissues |
| Growth hormone | Anterior pituitary | Raises | Anti-insulin action |
| Thyroxine | Thyroid | Raises | ↑ absorption from gut, ↑ glycogenolysis |

```text
After a meal: glucose ↑ → insulin ↑ → glucose enters cells, stored as glycogen and fat → glucose ↓
During fasting: glucose ↓ → glucagon ↑ (and cortisol, adrenaline) → liver releases glucose
                (glycogenolysis first, gluconeogenesis later) → glucose ↑
```

**Organs**: the **liver** is the glucose "buffer" — it stores glucose after meals and releases it in fasting; muscle and adipose tissue take up glucose under insulin; the kidney excretes glucose above the threshold and contributes to gluconeogenesis in prolonged fasting.

## 1.7 Diabetes mellitus

**Definition**: a group of metabolic disorders marked by chronic hyperglycaemia due to a defect in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both, with disturbed metabolism of carbohydrate, fat and protein.

**Types**

| Feature | Type 1 | Type 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Autoimmune destruction of β cells → absolute insulin deficiency | Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency |
| Usual age | Children, young adults | Adults (now seen in young people too) |
| Body build | Usually thin | Often overweight/obese, central obesity |
| Onset | Sudden | Gradual; often found on a routine test |
| Ketoacidosis | Common | Uncommon (hyperosmolar state more typical) |
| Family history | Less strong | Strong |
| Treatment | Insulin always needed | Diet, exercise, oral drugs; insulin later in some |

Other types: **gestational diabetes** (first found in pregnancy), and diabetes due to other causes (pancreatitis, drugs such as steroids, endocrine disorders).

**Biochemical basis of the symptoms**

| Symptom | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| **Polyuria** (passing much urine) | Glucose above the renal threshold spills into urine and pulls water with it (osmotic diuresis) |
| **Polydipsia** (excess thirst) | Water lost in urine → dehydration |
| **Polyphagia** (excess hunger) | Cells are "starved" of glucose despite high blood glucose |
| Weight loss | Fat and protein broken down for energy |
| Tiredness, weakness | Poor glucose use by cells |
| Blurred vision, infections (boils, thrush, UTI), slow wound healing | High glucose damages lens function, immunity and healing |

**Complications**

| Acute | Chronic — small vessels (microvascular) | Chronic — large vessels (macrovascular) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): high glucose, ketone bodies, metabolic acidosis, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath | Retinopathy (can lead to blindness) | Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction |
| Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (very high glucose, severe dehydration, little ketosis) | Nephropathy (microalbuminuria → proteinuria → kidney failure) | Stroke |
| Hypoglycaemia (from treatment) | Neuropathy (numb feet, autonomic problems) | Peripheral vascular disease → diabetic foot, gangrene |

**Biochemistry of DKA**: no insulin → fat breakdown ↑ → fatty acids flood the liver → excess acetyl-CoA → **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) → metabolic acidosis (Unit 5); glucose high → osmotic diuresis → dehydration and loss of sodium and potassium.

**Management in brief**

1. **Diet**: regular meals, complex carbohydrates and fibre, limited sugar and saturated fat, portion control.
2. **Exercise**: regular moderate activity improves insulin sensitivity.
3. **Drugs**: oral glucose-lowering drugs (for example metformin, sulphonylureas and newer groups) in type 2; insulin in type 1 and when needed in type 2. Doses are decided by the doctor.
4. **Monitoring**: self blood glucose testing with a glucometer, HbA1c every few months, yearly eye, kidney (urine albumin, creatinine) and foot check, lipid profile and blood pressure.
5. **Education**: recognising and treating hypoglycaemia, sick-day care, foot care, insulin storage and injection technique, stopping smoking.

## 1.8 Investigations of diabetes mellitus

| Test | What it is | Diabetes if (about) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) | After 8 hours with no calories | ≥ 126 mg/dL |
| 2-hour plasma glucose in OGTT | 2 h after a 75 g glucose drink | ≥ 200 mg/dL |
| Random plasma glucose | Any time | ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms |
| HbA1c | Glycated haemoglobin | ≥ 6.5% |

"Prediabetes" (increased risk): FPG about 100–125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose) or 2-h OGTT value about 140–199 mg/dL (impaired glucose tolerance). (WHO uses 110–125 mg/dL for impaired fasting glucose.)

Other tests: urine glucose and ketones (Benedict's test, dipsticks, Rothera's test for ketones), urine microalbumin, serum creatinine, lipid profile, C-peptide (to judge the patient's own insulin output).

## 1.9 Glucose tolerance test (OGTT)

**Definition**: a test of the body's ability to handle a standard glucose load; blood glucose is measured fasting and at fixed times after drinking glucose.

**Indications**

- Borderline fasting or random glucose values (doubtful diabetes)
- Glucose in urine without symptoms (to separate diabetes from renal glycosuria)
- Screening and diagnosis of gestational diabetes
- People at high risk: strong family history, obesity, a previous large baby
- Unexplained recurrent infections, retinopathy or neuropathy

**Procedure (the steps a student learns, with reasons)**

1. **Preparation for 3 days**: normal diet with adequate carbohydrate (about 150 g/day) and normal activity. *Reason*: a low-carbohydrate diet reduces tolerance and gives a falsely "diabetic" curve.
2. **Overnight fast of 8–14 hours** (water allowed). *Reason*: a true fasting baseline.
3. Avoid smoking, tea/coffee and exercise on the test morning; the patient sits quietly throughout. Note drugs that affect glucose (steroids, diuretics) for the doctor. *Reason*: these change glucose values.
4. Collect a **fasting blood sample** (in a fluoride tube) and a **fasting urine sample**. *Reason*: fluoride stops RBCs using glucose in the tube.
5. Give **75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in about 250–300 mL water**, to be drunk within 5 minutes (children: 1.75 g per kg body weight, not more than 75 g). Note the time.
6. Collect blood (and urine) samples at **30-minute intervals for 2 hours** (classic test), or at least at **2 hours** (WHO standard test).
7. Label each tube with name, time and sample number; send promptly.
8. Watch for faintness, nausea or vomiting (vomiting spoils the test); report it.

**Interpretation (venous plasma, about)**

| Result | Fasting | 2 hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | below 100 mg/dL | below 140 mg/dL |
| Impaired glucose tolerance | below 126 | 140–199 |
| Diabetes mellitus | ≥ 126 | ≥ 200 |

In a normal curve the value peaks within 30–60 minutes (usually below about 160–180 mg/dL), returns to the fasting level by about 2 hours, and no glucose appears in urine.

**Types of GTT curve**

```text
Plasma glucose (mg/dL), sampled at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min

            0 min    30–60 min (peak)    120 min     Urine glucose
Normal      <100     <160–180            <140        absent
Impaired    <126     raised              140–199     usually absent
Diabetic    ≥126     very high           ≥200        present
Lag curve   normal   >180 (sharp peak)   normal      present briefly
Flat curve  normal   small rise only     normal      absent

Draw it as a graph in the exam: time on the x-axis, glucose on the y-axis,
a dotted line at about 180 mg/dL for the renal threshold.
```

| Curve | Pattern | Seen in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Peak within 1 h below renal threshold; fasting level by 2 h | Healthy person |
| Diabetic | High fasting, high peak, still high at 2 h; glycosuria | Diabetes mellitus |
| Impaired | In between normal and diabetic | Prediabetes |
| **Lag (alimentary / "oxyhyperglycaemic") curve** | Quick high peak above renal threshold at 30–60 min, normal at 2 h, brief glycosuria | After gastrectomy (fast emptying), hyperthyroidism, some liver disease |
| **Renal glycosuria** | Normal blood curve but glucose in urine | Low renal threshold (harmless tubular defect, pregnancy) |
| **Flat curve** | Very small rise | Malabsorption, hypothyroidism, Addison's disease, hypopituitarism |

## 1.10 Variants of the GTT

| Variant | How it differs | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mini GTT** | Only two blood (and urine) samples: fasting and 2 hours after 75 g glucose | Routine screening; quicker and cheaper; the form used most in practice |
| **Extended GTT** | Sampling continued every 30–60 min up to 4–6 hours | Suspected reactive (post-meal) hypoglycaemia, where glucose falls low 3–5 h after the load |
| **Glucose challenge test (GCT)** | 50 g glucose given at any time of day without fasting; one sample at 1 hour | Screening for gestational diabetes; a raised value (commonly ≥ 140 mg/dL) is followed by a full OGTT |
| **Intravenous GTT** | Glucose is given into a vein and blood sampled at intervals | When oral absorption is unreliable: malabsorption, after gastric surgery, persistent vomiting |

**Gestational diabetes in India**: national guidelines use a single-step 75 g oral glucose test in pregnancy with a 2-hour value. Check the current Ministry of Health guideline for the exact timing and cut-off used in your hospital.

## 1.11 HbA1c (definition only)

**HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin)** is haemoglobin A to which glucose has attached itself non-enzymatically (glycation). Because red cells live about 120 days, the percentage of HbA1c reflects the **average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months**. A value of about 6.5% or above supports a diagnosis of diabetes; below about 5.7% is usually normal. It does not need fasting. It can be misleading in anaemia, haemoglobin variants and after blood loss or transfusion.

## 1.12 Hypoglycaemia

**Definition**: a blood glucose low enough to cause symptoms or harm; in practice a plasma glucose below about **70 mg/dL** is treated as hypoglycaemia (alert value), and below about 54 mg/dL is significant. Classic proof is **Whipple's triad**: symptoms of hypoglycaemia, a low measured glucose at that time, and relief when glucose is raised.

**Causes**

- **Drug-induced** (commonest): excess insulin or sulphonylurea, a missed or late meal, unusual exercise
- Alcohol (blocks gluconeogenesis), especially on an empty stomach
- Insulinoma (insulin-secreting tumour)
- Liver failure (cannot release or make glucose), severe sepsis
- Adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism (lack of counter-regulatory hormones)
- Starvation, severe malnutrition
- Inborn errors: glycogen storage disease, galactosaemia, hereditary fructose intolerance
- Newborns: infants of diabetic mothers, preterm and small-for-date babies
- Reactive hypoglycaemia after meals, after gastric surgery

**Features**: sweating, tremor, palpitation, hunger, anxiety (adrenaline response); then confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, fits and coma (brain deprived of glucose).

## 1.13 Application in nursing

- Check capillary blood glucose with a glucometer: clean and dry the fingertip (alcohol left on the skin alters the reading), prick the side of the finger, wipe the first drop, record time and relation to meals.
- Collect glucose samples in **fluoride (grey-top) tubes**; delay in plain tubes lowers the value as cells keep using glucose.
- Know the signs of hypoglycaemia and the hospital protocol to give quick-acting sugar to a conscious patient; recheck glucose.
- Watch a diabetic patient for DKA: rising glucose, ketones in urine, deep rapid breathing, vomiting, dehydration.
- Teach foot care, regular meals with insulin, sick-day rules and the meaning of HbA1c.
- Prepare patients correctly for OGTT; the result is only as good as the preparation.

## Remember

- End products of carbohydrate digestion: glucose, fructose, galactose; glucose and galactose absorbed with sodium (SGLT-1).
- Glycolysis: cytoplasm, net 2 ATP, works without oxygen; RBCs depend on it.
- Insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose.
- Renal threshold for glucose is about 180 mg/dL.
- Diabetes (about): FPG ≥ 126, 2-h OGTT ≥ 200, random ≥ 200 with symptoms, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.
- OGTT: 3 days normal carbohydrate diet, overnight fast, 75 g glucose in about 250–300 mL water, samples fasting to 2 h.
- Lag curve = early high peak with brief glycosuria (gastrectomy, hyperthyroidism); flat curve = malabsorption, hypothyroidism, Addison's.
- Mini GTT = fasting + 2 h samples; GCT = 50 g, non-fasting, 1 h sample.
- HbA1c = glycated haemoglobin, average glucose over 2–3 months.
- Hypoglycaemia below about 70 mg/dL; Whipple's triad; commonest cause is diabetes treatment.
