# Unit 2: Lipids, lipoproteins and atherosclerosis

INC Unit II (8 hours): fatty acids (definition, classification); MUFA, PUFA, essential and trans fatty acids; digestion, absorption and metabolism of lipids and related disorders; compounds formed from cholesterol; ketone bodies (names, types and significance only); lipoproteins (types and functions — their metabolism is not required); lipid profile; atherosclerosis in brief.

> Lipid values in these notes are approximate ("about") and follow commonly used adult targets. Laboratories and cardiology guidelines differ; read every report against its own reference range.

## 2.1 What lipids are

Lipids are a mixed group of compounds that are insoluble in water and soluble in fat solvents (ether, chloroform), and are used or stored by living cells.

| Group | Examples | Main role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple lipids | Triacylglycerols (fats and oils), waxes | Stored energy (9 kcal per gram) |
| Compound lipids | Phospholipids (lecithin), glycolipids, lipoproteins | Cell membranes, nerve tissue, transport |
| Derived lipids | Fatty acids, cholesterol, steroid hormones, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) | Fuel, hormones, vitamins |

Fat also insulates the body, cushions organs and carries fat-soluble vitamins.

## 2.2 Fatty acids

**Definition**: fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group (–COOH) at one end. In nature they usually have an even number of carbon atoms and are found mostly as esters (in triacylglycerols and phospholipids), not free.

**Classification**

| Basis | Groups | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chain length (approximate) | Short chain (up to 6 C), medium chain (8–12 C), long chain (14 C and more) | Butyric (butter); caprylic (coconut oil); palmitic, stearic |
| Saturation | **Saturated** — no double bond | Palmitic (16 C), stearic (18 C) |
| | **Monounsaturated (MUFA)** — one double bond | Oleic acid (18 C, ω-9) |
| | **Polyunsaturated (PUFA)** — two or more double bonds | Linoleic (ω-6), α-linolenic (ω-3), arachidonic (ω-6), EPA and DHA (ω-3) |
| Nutritional need | **Essential** — must come from diet | Linoleic, α-linolenic (arachidonic becomes essential if linoleic is lacking) |
| | Non-essential — body can make them | Palmitic, oleic |
| Shape at the double bond | **Cis** (natural form, chain bends) or **trans** (chain straight) | Most natural oils are cis; trans fats come mainly from partially hydrogenated oil |

The "ω" (omega) number tells where the first double bond is, counted from the methyl (far) end.

**Clinical significance**

| Type | Main sources | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **MUFA** | Olive oil, groundnut oil, mustard oil, rice-bran oil, nuts | Lower LDL cholesterol without lowering HDL; protective for the heart |
| **PUFA (ω-6)** | Sunflower, safflower, soyabean, corn oils | Lower LDL; very high intake of ω-6 alone is not advised |
| **PUFA (ω-3)** | Fish and fish oil (EPA, DHA), flaxseed, mustard oil, walnuts | Lower triglycerides, reduce clotting and inflammation; DHA important for brain and retina of the foetus and infant |
| **Essential fatty acids** | Vegetable oils | Needed for cell membranes, skin barrier, and to make eicosanoids (prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes); deficiency causes dry scaly skin (phrynoderma, "toad skin"), poor growth, poor wound healing, fatty liver |
| **Trans fatty acids** | Vanaspati, some margarines, bakery and deep-fried foods, re-used frying oil | **Raise LDL and lower HDL** — the most harmful dietary fat; increase coronary heart disease risk. India's food regulator (FSSAI) limits trans fat in edible oils and fats — check the current permitted level |

Saturated fats (ghee, butter, coconut and palm oil, red meat) raise LDL cholesterol when eaten in excess.

## 2.3 Digestion and absorption of lipids

```text
MOUTH/STOMACH  Lingual and gastric lipase — minor (more important in infants: milk fat)
DUODENUM       Bile salts (from liver via gall bladder) EMULSIFY fat into small droplets
               Pancreatic lipase (+ colipase) → triacylglycerol → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 fatty acids
               Cholesterol esterase → cholesterol esters → cholesterol + fatty acid
               Phospholipase A2 → phospholipids → lysophospholipid + fatty acid
JEJUNUM        Products + bile salts form MICELLES → reach the brush border → enter cells
INSIDE CELL    Long-chain fatty acids re-made into triacylglycerol + cholesterol esters
               + apoprotein B-48 → CHYLOMICRONS → lacteals (lymph) → thoracic duct → blood
               Short- and medium-chain fatty acids → straight into portal blood
BILE SALTS     Reabsorbed in the ileum and returned to the liver (enterohepatic circulation)
```

**Clinical points**

- No bile (obstructive jaundice) or no pancreatic lipase (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) → fat is not absorbed → **steatorrhoea** (bulky, pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float) and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K (bleeding from vitamin K deficiency).
- Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil is used in diets for fat malabsorption because it needs little bile or lipase and goes directly to portal blood.

## 2.4 Metabolism of lipids

| Process | Site | Summary | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Lipolysis** | Adipose tissue | Stored triacylglycerol → glycerol + free fatty acids | Hormone-sensitive lipase; activated by adrenaline, glucagon, cortisol; inhibited by insulin |
| **β-oxidation of fatty acids** | Mitochondria (liver, muscle, heart) | Fatty acid broken two carbons at a time → acetyl-CoA, NADH, FADH2 | Long-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria with **carnitine**; high energy yield (palmitate gives about 106 ATP); brain and RBCs cannot use fatty acids |
| **Fatty acid synthesis** | Cytoplasm (liver, adipose, lactating breast) | Acetyl-CoA → fatty acids | Needs NADPH (from HMP shunt) and biotin; stimulated by insulin and a carbohydrate-rich diet |
| **Triacylglycerol synthesis** | Liver, adipose | Glycerol-3-phosphate + fatty acids | Liver exports it as VLDL |
| **Cholesterol synthesis** | Liver mainly (all nucleated cells can) | Acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonate → … → cholesterol | Rate-limiting enzyme **HMG-CoA reductase**, the target of statin drugs |
| **Ketogenesis** | Liver mitochondria only | Excess acetyl-CoA → ketone bodies | See 2.6 |
| **Phospholipid metabolism** | Most tissues | Lecithin, sphingomyelin etc. | Lung surfactant is mainly dipalmitoyl lecithin |

Glycerol from fat can be made into glucose (gluconeogenesis), but fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose.

## 2.5 Disorders of lipid metabolism

| Disorder | Basis | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Obesity** | Energy intake more than use → fat storage | Risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, fatty liver |
| **Fatty liver** | Fat made or brought to the liver faster than exported as VLDL | Alcohol, obesity, diabetes, protein deficiency (kwashiorkor) and lack of choline/methionine (**lipotropic factors**); can progress to cirrhosis |
| **Hyperlipoproteinaemias / dyslipidaemias** | Raised cholesterol and/or triglycerides (primary inherited types I–V, or secondary to diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, alcohol) | Premature atherosclerosis, xanthomas; very high triglycerides cause acute pancreatitis |
| **Familial hypercholesterolaemia** | Defective LDL receptors | Very high LDL, tendon xanthomas, heart attacks at a young age |
| **Ketosis / ketoacidosis** | Excess ketone bodies | Starvation, uncontrolled diabetes (see 2.6) |
| **Lipid storage diseases (sphingolipidoses)** | Inherited lysosomal enzyme defects | Tay-Sachs disease (nerve degeneration, cherry-red spot), Gaucher's disease (large spleen, bone pain), Niemann-Pick disease |
| **Steatorrhoea** | Poor digestion/absorption | See 2.3 |
| **Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn** | Lack of lung surfactant in preterm babies | Alveoli collapse |

## 2.6 Ketone bodies (names, types and significance)

**Names**: three compounds made in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA:

| Ketone body | Type | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Acetoacetate** | Primary ketone body (a keto acid) | The first one formed |
| **β-hydroxybutyrate** | Formed from acetoacetate by reduction (strictly a hydroxy acid, not a ketone) | Main ketone body in blood in ketoacidosis |
| **Acetone** | Formed by loss of CO2 from acetoacetate; volatile | Breathed out — gives the **fruity breath** in ketoacidosis |

**Significance**

1. **Normal fuel**: heart muscle, skeletal muscle and kidney use ketone bodies; in prolonged starvation the **brain** adapts to use them, sparing body protein. The liver makes them but cannot use them.
2. **Ketosis**: increased ketone bodies in blood (ketonaemia) and urine (ketonuria) when fat breakdown is high and carbohydrate is unavailable — **starvation, prolonged fasting or vomiting, uncontrolled diabetes**, very low-carbohydrate diets, alcohol excess.
3. **Ketoacidosis**: acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids; in excess they use up bicarbonate → metabolic acidosis with high anion gap (diabetic ketoacidosis). Features: vomiting, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, drowsiness, coma.
4. **Detection**: **Rothera's test** (sodium nitroprusside) and urine dipsticks give a purple colour with acetoacetate and acetone; they **do not detect β-hydroxybutyrate**, so a urine test can underestimate ketosis.

## 2.7 Compounds formed from cholesterol

Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol found only in animal foods (egg yolk, meat, organ meats, butter, ghee). The body also makes it in the liver.

```text
                       ┌─→ Bile acids and bile salts (cholic, chenodeoxycholic acid) — fat digestion
                       │       (main route of cholesterol removal from the body)
                       ├─→ Steroid hormones:
CHOLESTEROL ───────────┤     • Glucocorticoids (cortisol)       — adrenal cortex
                       │     • Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) — adrenal cortex
                       │     • Sex hormones: progesterone, testosterone, oestrogens
                       ├─→ Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) — 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin + sunlight (UV)
                       └─→ Part of cell membranes and myelin; cholesterol esters for storage
```

## 2.8 Lipoproteins — types and functions

Lipids do not dissolve in plasma, so they travel as **lipoproteins**: a core of triacylglycerol and cholesterol esters, covered by a shell of phospholipid, free cholesterol and proteins called **apolipoproteins** (apo B-48, B-100, A-I, C-II, E).

| Lipoprotein | Made in | Main lipid carried | Function | Density |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Chylomicrons** | Intestine | Dietary triacylglycerol | Carry dietary fat from gut to tissues (muscle, adipose); remnants to liver | Lowest density, largest |
| **VLDL** (very low density) | Liver | Endogenous triacylglycerol | Carry fat made in the liver to tissues | Very low |
| **IDL** (intermediate) | From VLDL | TG and cholesterol | Short-lived; becomes LDL | Low |
| **LDL** (low density) | From VLDL/IDL in blood | **Cholesterol** (richest in cholesterol) | Carry cholesterol to tissues; excess enters artery walls → atherosclerosis ("**bad cholesterol**") | Low |
| **HDL** (high density) | Liver, intestine | Protein-rich; collects cholesterol | **Reverse cholesterol transport** — takes excess cholesterol from tissues back to the liver; protective ("**good cholesterol**") | Highest density, smallest |

On electrophoresis, HDL moves as α-lipoprotein, LDL as β-lipoprotein, VLDL as pre-β; chylomicrons stay at the origin. **Lipoprotein (a)** is an LDL-like particle; a high level is an inherited risk for heart disease.

## 2.9 Lipid profile

**Preparation**: classically a 10–12 hour overnight fast (water allowed), because triacylglycerol rises after a meal. Many labs now accept non-fasting samples for cholesterol; follow the lab instruction. Avoid alcohol and heavy fatty meals the day before.

| Parameter | Desirable / normal (adults, about) |
| --- | --- |
| Total cholesterol | below 200 mg/dL |
| LDL cholesterol | below 100 mg/dL (optimal); 160 and above is high |
| HDL cholesterol | above 40 mg/dL in men and above 50 mg/dL in women; 60 and above is protective |
| Triacylglycerols (triglycerides) | below 150 mg/dL |
| VLDL cholesterol | about 5–40 mg/dL (calculated as TG ÷ 5) |
| Total cholesterol : HDL ratio | below about 4.5–5 |

**Friedewald formula** (all in mg/dL; valid when TG is below about 400):

```text
LDL cholesterol = Total cholesterol − HDL cholesterol − (Triglycerides ÷ 5)

Example: TC 220, HDL 40, TG 150 → LDL = 220 − 40 − 30 = 150 mg/dL (high)
```

People with diabetes or known heart disease are given lower LDL targets by their doctors.

## 2.10 Atherosclerosis (in brief)

**Definition**: a disease of large and medium arteries in which lipid-rich plaques (atheromas) form in the inner wall (intima), narrowing the lumen and making the wall hard and fragile.

**Risk factors**

- Cannot change: increasing age, male sex, family history, genetic dyslipidaemia
- Can change: high LDL, low HDL, high triglycerides, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, diet rich in saturated and trans fat, stress

**How it develops**

```text
Damage to the endothelium (high BP, smoking, high glucose, high LDL)
        ↓
LDL enters the intima and is oxidised
        ↓
Monocytes enter → become macrophages → swallow oxidised LDL → FOAM CELLS
        ↓
Fatty streak (earliest visible lesion, even in young people)
        ↓
Smooth muscle cells move in, make collagen → FIBROUS PLAQUE (fibrous cap over a lipid core)
        ↓
Calcification, narrowing; cap may RUPTURE → platelet clot (thrombus) → sudden blockage
```

**Results**: angina and myocardial infarction (coronary arteries), stroke (cerebral/carotid arteries), peripheral vascular disease and gangrene (leg arteries), aneurysm (aorta), renal artery stenosis.

**Prevention and nursing role**: teach a diet low in saturated and trans fat and rich in fibre, fruits and vegetables and MUFA/PUFA oils; regular exercise; weight control; stopping smoking; control of blood pressure, diabetes and lipids (statins as prescribed); regular lipid profile checks.

## 2.11 Application in nursing

- Prepare patients correctly for a lipid profile (fasting if the lab asks; note recent illness, since values fall after an acute illness or MI).
- Check urine for ketones in diabetic, vomiting or starving patients; remember the dipstick misses β-hydroxybutyrate.
- In obstructive jaundice and pancreatic disease, watch for steatorrhoea and bleeding (vitamin K).
- Diet counselling: limit vanaspati, re-used frying oil and bakery products (trans fat); use a mix of oils; include fish or other ω-3 sources.
- Preterm babies may lack surfactant (a phospholipid); antenatal steroids given to the mother help the lungs mature.

## Remember

- Fatty acid = hydrocarbon chain with –COOH; MUFA has one double bond (oleic), PUFA two or more (linoleic, linolenic, arachidonic).
- Essential fatty acids: linoleic and α-linolenic; deficiency → phrynoderma.
- Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL — the worst dietary fat.
- Fat digestion needs bile salts (emulsify) and pancreatic lipase; long-chain fats travel as chylomicrons in lymph.
- β-oxidation is in mitochondria and needs carnitine; HMG-CoA reductase controls cholesterol synthesis.
- Ketone bodies: acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone; made in liver, used by heart, muscle, kidney and (in starvation) brain; Rothera's test misses β-hydroxybutyrate.
- From cholesterol: bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D3.
- Chylomicrons — dietary fat; VLDL — liver fat; LDL — cholesterol to tissues (bad); HDL — reverse transport (good).
- Desirable (about): total cholesterol <200, LDL <100, HDL >40 (men)/>50 (women), TG <150 mg/dL; LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5.
- Atherosclerosis: endothelial injury → oxidised LDL → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → rupture and clot.

# Unit 3: Amino acids, proteins and plasma proteins

INC Unit III (9 hours): classification of amino acids by nutritional need and metabolic fate; digestion, absorption and metabolism of proteins and related disorders; biologically important compounds made from amino acids (names only); inborn errors of aromatic amino acid metabolism (in brief); plasma proteins — types, functions and normal values; causes of proteinuria, hypoproteinaemia and hypergammaglobulinaemia; principle of electrophoresis with normal and abnormal patterns (in brief).

> Normal values here are approximate ("about"); each laboratory prints its own range.

## 3.1 Amino acids and proteins

**Amino acids** are the building blocks of proteins. Each has an amino group (–NH2), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen and a side chain (R group) attached to one carbon. Twenty amino acids are used to build human proteins. They are joined by **peptide bonds** to form peptides and proteins.

**Proteins** do almost everything in the body: enzymes, structure (collagen, keratin), transport (haemoglobin, albumin), defence (antibodies), hormones (insulin), clotting (fibrinogen), muscle contraction (actin, myosin) and buffering. Protein gives 4 kcal per gram. Protein is the only major food that supplies **nitrogen**.

## 3.2 Classification of amino acids

### By nutritional requirement

| Group | Meaning | Amino acids |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Essential** | Cannot be made in the body; must come from food | Valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine |
| **Semi-essential** (conditionally essential) | Body makes them, but not enough during growth | **Arginine, histidine** (needed in the diet of growing children) |
| **Non-essential** | Body can make them | Glycine, alanine, serine, aspartate, glutamate, asparagine, glutamine, proline, tyrosine, cysteine |

Memory aid for the ten (essential + semi-essential): **"PVT TIM HALL"** — Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine, Leucine, Lysine.

A protein containing all essential amino acids in good proportion (egg, milk, meat, fish) is a **complete / first-class protein**. Cereals are low in lysine and pulses are low in methionine; eating them together (dal + rice, khichdi) makes up the gap — the **supplementary value of proteins**.

### By metabolic fate

The carbon skeleton left after removing the amino group can become glucose, ketone bodies, or both.

| Group | What the skeleton forms | Amino acids |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Purely ketogenic** | Acetyl-CoA / acetoacetate (ketone bodies, fat) | Leucine, lysine |
| **Both ketogenic and glucogenic** | Both | Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan (threonine is placed here in some books) |
| **Purely glucogenic** | Glucose (by gluconeogenesis) | All the rest — e.g. alanine, glycine, serine, glutamate, aspartate, methionine, valine, histidine, arginine |

Other useful groups: aromatic (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan), sulphur-containing (methionine, cysteine), branched-chain (valine, leucine, isoleucine), acidic (aspartate, glutamate), basic (lysine, arginine, histidine).

## 3.3 Digestion of proteins

| Site | Enzyme (inactive form → active) | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stomach | Pepsinogen → **pepsin** (activated by HCl) | Breaks proteins into large peptides; HCl also denatures protein |
| Stomach (infants) | **Rennin** | Clots milk protein (casein) so it stays longer in the stomach |
| Small intestine (pancreatic juice) | Trypsinogen → **trypsin** (by enteropeptidase/enterokinase of the gut wall); trypsin then activates the others | Trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase cut inside the chain (endopeptidases); carboxypeptidase cuts from the carboxyl end |
| Small intestine (brush border) | Aminopeptidases, dipeptidases, tripeptidases | Cut small peptides into free amino acids |

Enzymes are released as **inactive precursors (zymogens)** so they do not digest the cells that make them. Early activation of trypsin inside the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.

## 3.4 Absorption

- Free amino acids are absorbed in the small intestine by **sodium-dependent active transport** (several carriers for different groups); di- and tripeptides are absorbed too and split inside the cell.
- A minor route, the **γ-glutamyl cycle** (glutathione-dependent), also carries amino acids into cells.
- Amino acids reach the **liver by the portal vein**.
- Newborns can absorb some whole proteins (antibodies in colostrum) for a short time after birth — the start of passive immunity; this is also how some food allergies may start.

## 3.5 Metabolism of amino acids and proteins

```text
          Dietary protein        Body protein breakdown
                 ↘                   ↙
                AMINO ACID POOL ──────→ Body proteins, enzymes, hormones,
                       │                 special products (3.7)
                       ↓
            Removal of the amino group
     (transamination + oxidative deamination)
          ↙                          ↘
   AMMONIA (NH3)               CARBON SKELETON
       ↓  liver                  → glucose, ketone bodies, energy (TCA cycle)
   UREA CYCLE → urea → kidney → urine
```

**Transamination**: the amino group is moved from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and a new keto acid. Enzymes are **aminotransferases (transaminases)**, which need **pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)**. Two of them are important in diagnosis: **ALT** (alanine aminotransferase) and **AST** (aspartate aminotransferase) — see Unit 4.

**Oxidative deamination**: glutamate dehydrogenase removes the amino group from glutamate as free **ammonia**, mainly in the liver.

**Transport of ammonia**: ammonia is toxic to the brain. It travels in blood mainly as **glutamine** (from most tissues) and **alanine** (from muscle) to the liver and kidney.

**Urea cycle (Krebs–Henseleit cycle)**: occurs **only in the liver**, partly in mitochondria and partly in the cytoplasm. Ammonia + CO2 + the amino group of aspartate → **urea**, which is carried in blood to the kidney and excreted. It uses energy (3 ATP per urea). Key enzymes: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I, ornithine transcarbamoylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, arginase.

```text
NH3 + CO2 → carbamoyl phosphate → (with ornithine) citrulline → (+ aspartate)
argininosuccinate → arginine (+ fumarate) → ARGININE splits → UREA + ornithine
(ornithine goes round again)
```

Urea is the main nitrogen-containing waste in urine. Blood urea rises in kidney failure and falls in severe liver failure.

**Nitrogen balance**: positive in growth, pregnancy and recovery (intake > loss); negative in starvation, fever, burns, surgery, uncontrolled diabetes and cancer wasting (loss > intake).

## 3.6 Disorders related to protein metabolism

| Disorder | Cause | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Protein–energy malnutrition** | Low protein/energy intake | **Kwashiorkor** (oedema due to low albumin, fatty liver, skin and hair changes) and **marasmus** (severe wasting, no oedema) |
| **Hyperammonaemia** | Liver failure or urea cycle enzyme defects | Vomiting, irritability, lethargy, flapping tremor, coma — ammonia poisons the brain; **hepatic encephalopathy** in cirrhosis |
| **Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism** | Missing enzyme | Phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria, albinism etc. (3.8) |
| **Gout** | High uric acid (end product of purine — not protein — breakdown, but often taught here) | Painful joints, tophi, kidney stones |
| **Cystinuria, Hartnup disease** | Defective amino acid transport in kidney/gut | Stones (cystine); pellagra-like rash (Hartnup) |
| **Proteinuria, hypoproteinaemia** | See 3.10 | |

## 3.7 Biologically important compounds made from amino acids (names only)

| Amino acid | Compounds formed |
| --- | --- |
| **Glycine** | Haem (with succinyl-CoA), creatine, glutathione, purines, bile salts (glycocholic acid) |
| **Tyrosine** (from phenylalanine) | Dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline (catecholamines); thyroxine (T4) and T3; melanin |
| **Tryptophan** | Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine), melatonin, niacin (vitamin B3) |
| **Histidine** | Histamine |
| **Arginine** | Nitric oxide, creatine, urea, ornithine (→ polyamines) |
| **Methionine** | S-adenosylmethionine (methyl donor), cysteine, creatine (methyl group) |
| **Cysteine** | Taurine (bile salts), glutathione |
| **Glutamate** | GABA (inhibitory brain transmitter), glutathione |
| **Aspartate, glutamine** | Purines and pyrimidines (DNA, RNA) |
| **Serine** | Ethanolamine, choline, sphingosine (phospholipids) |

## 3.8 Inborn errors of aromatic amino acid metabolism (in brief)

```text
Phenylalanine ──(phenylalanine hydroxylase)──→ Tyrosine ──→ Homogentisic acid ──(homogentisate oxidase)──→ ... → fumarate + acetoacetate
      ✗ PKU                                     │      ✗ tyrosinaemia                ✗ alkaptonuria
                                                ├──(tyrosinase)──→ Melanin   ✗ albinism
                                                ├──→ Dopamine → noradrenaline → adrenaline
                                                └──→ Thyroxine
```

| Disease | Missing enzyme | Main features | Management in brief |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Phenylketonuria (PKU)** | Phenylalanine hydroxylase | Phenylalanine and phenylketones build up → **intellectual disability**, fits, hyperactivity, **mousy (musty) body odour**, fair skin and hair (less melanin), eczema; mother with uncontrolled PKU harms the foetus | **Newborn screening** (Guthrie test or modern blood spot methods); lifelong **low-phenylalanine diet** started early; avoid aspartame-sweetened products |
| **Alkaptonuria** | Homogentisate oxidase | Homogentisic acid in urine → **urine turns black on standing** (alkaline/air oxidation); dark pigment in cartilage, sclera and ears (**ochronosis**); arthritis in adult life | Usually mild in childhood; supportive treatment |
| **Albinism** | Tyrosinase (in melanocytes) | No melanin: white hair, pale skin, pink/pale irises, **photophobia**, poor vision, nystagmus, high risk of skin cancer and sunburn | Protect from sun (clothing, sunscreen, dark glasses); eye care |
| **Tyrosinaemia** (type I) | Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (later step) | Liver failure, kidney tubular defects, cabbage-like odour | Special diet and specific drug under specialist care |

Tryptophan: **Hartnup disease** (defective absorption of tryptophan) gives a pellagra-like skin rash, because less tryptophan is available for niacin.

## 3.9 Plasma proteins — types, functions and normal values

Plasma proteins are separated into **albumin, globulins (α1, α2, β, γ) and fibrinogen**. Most are made in the **liver**; immunoglobulins (γ-globulins) are made by **plasma cells** (B lymphocytes).

**Normal values (serum, adults, about)**

| Protein | About |
| --- | --- |
| Total protein | 6.0–8.0 g/dL |
| Albumin | 3.5–5.0 g/dL |
| Globulin | 2.0–3.5 g/dL |
| Albumin : globulin (A:G) ratio | normally above 1; commonly about 1.5–2 : 1 (falls below 1, "reversed", in cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome and myeloma) |
| Fibrinogen (plasma) | 200–400 mg/dL |

Serum = plasma minus clotting proteins (fibrinogen).

**Types and functions**

| Protein | Examples | Functions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Albumin** (largest share, smallest molecule) | — | Maintains **colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure** (about 80% of it) and so holds water in vessels; transports bilirubin, free fatty acids, calcium, hormones (thyroxine), many drugs; buffer; source of amino acids in starvation |
| **α1-globulins** | α1-antitrypsin, α1-acid glycoprotein, α1-lipoprotein (HDL) | α1-antitrypsin protects the lung from enzyme damage (its deficiency → emphysema, liver disease) |
| **α2-globulins** | Haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, α2-macroglobulin | Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin (falls in haemolysis); ceruloplasmin carries copper (low in Wilson's disease) |
| **β-globulins** | Transferrin, β-lipoprotein (LDL), complement C3, haemopexin | Transferrin carries iron (rises in iron deficiency) |
| **γ-globulins** | Immunoglobulins IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE | Antibodies — defence (Unit 7) |
| **Fibrinogen** and other clotting factors | Factor I, prothrombin | Blood clotting |
| **Acute phase proteins** | C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin rise; albumin and transferrin fall | Rise within hours of infection, injury or inflammation — CRP is a common marker of inflammation |

**Albumin and oedema**: when albumin falls below about 2.5 g/dL the oncotic pressure falls, fluid leaks from capillaries into tissues → **oedema** (puffy face, ankles) and ascites (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, kwashiorkor).

## 3.10 Proteinuria, hypoproteinaemia and hypergammaglobulinaemia

### Proteinuria

Normal urine contains very little protein (less than about **150 mg per day**). More than this is **proteinuria**. **Microalbuminuria** (albumin about 30–300 mg/day) is an early sign of kidney damage in diabetes and hypertension.

| Type | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| Physiological / functional (temporary) | Heavy exercise, fever, cold exposure, emotional stress, **orthostatic (postural) proteinuria** in young people on standing, pregnancy |
| **Glomerular** (filtration barrier damaged — mostly albumin) | Nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, **diabetic nephropathy**, hypertension, **pre-eclampsia**, SLE |
| **Tubular** (small proteins not reabsorbed) | Tubular damage from heavy metals, some drugs, pyelonephritis |
| **Overflow (pre-renal)** | Small proteins in excess in blood: **Bence Jones protein** (light chains) in multiple myeloma, haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis), myoglobinuria (crush injury) |
| **Post-renal** | Urinary tract infection, stones, tumours of the bladder/urethra, blood in urine |

Tests: dipstick, heat and acetic acid test, sulphosalicylic acid test, 24-hour urine protein, urine albumin : creatinine ratio. Bence Jones protein precipitates at about 40–60 °C, redissolves near boiling and reappears on cooling.

### Hypoproteinaemia (low total plasma protein, mostly low albumin)

| Mechanism | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| Low intake | Starvation, protein–energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) |
| Poor digestion/absorption | Malabsorption, chronic pancreatitis |
| Low synthesis | **Liver disease** (cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis) |
| Increased loss | **Nephrotic syndrome** (urine), **burns** (skin), protein-losing enteropathy (gut), haemorrhage, repeated tapping of ascites |
| Increased breakdown | Fever, sepsis, cancer, thyrotoxicosis, after major surgery |
| Dilution | Over-hydration, pregnancy (mild, physiological) |

### Hypergammaglobulinaemia (raised γ-globulins)

| Type | Pattern | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Polyclonal** | Broad rise of many antibodies | Chronic infections (tuberculosis, kala-azar, chronic osteomyelitis, HIV), **chronic liver disease (cirrhosis)**, autoimmune disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), sarcoidosis |
| **Monoclonal** (paraproteinaemia) | One clone of plasma cells makes one protein → sharp narrow **M band** | **Multiple myeloma**, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (IgM), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance |

## 3.11 Electrophoresis (in brief)

**Principle**: charged particles move in an electric field. At an alkaline pH (about 8.6, barbital buffer) plasma proteins carry a **negative charge** and move towards the **anode (+)**. Each protein moves at a speed that depends on its net charge, size and shape, so proteins separate into bands.

**Method in short**: a small drop of serum is applied on a strip (cellulose acetate or agarose gel) soaked in buffer → current passed for a set time → strip stained (e.g. amido black or Ponceau S) → bands seen and measured by a densitometer as peaks.

**Normal pattern** (from anode to cathode — fastest to slowest):

```text
 (+) Anode                                              Cathode (−)
     │ ALBUMIN │  α1  │   α2   │   β   │      γ       │ origin
     │  tall,  │ faint│ moderate│moderate│  broad,     │ (serum applied)
     │  sharp  │      │         │        │  diffuse    │
     5 bands in serum; plasma shows an extra fibrinogen band between β and γ
```

**Abnormal patterns**

| Condition | Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| **Nephrotic syndrome** | Albumin markedly ↓, **α2 ↑** (α2-macroglobulin retained), γ ↓ or normal |
| **Cirrhosis of liver** | Albumin ↓, broad polyclonal γ ↑, with **β–γ bridging** (no gap between β and γ) |
| **Multiple myeloma** | A tall, narrow **M band (spike)** usually in the γ region; other γ often ↓ |
| **Chronic infection / inflammation** | Broad polyclonal **γ ↑** (sometimes α2 ↑) |
| **Acute inflammation** | α1 and α2 ↑ (acute phase proteins) |
| **α1-antitrypsin deficiency** | α1 band very faint or absent |
| **Agammaglobulinaemia** | γ band absent or very faint |

## 3.12 Application in nursing

- Check urine for protein (dipstick) in antenatal visits — proteinuria with high blood pressure suggests pre-eclampsia.
- Collect a correct 24-hour urine: discard the first morning sample, then collect every sample for 24 hours including the next morning's first sample; keep cool; record start and end times.
- Weigh daily and look for oedema in patients with low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition); give the diet advised.
- In liver failure, watch for confusion and flapping tremor (rising ammonia); protein intake is adjusted by the doctor/dietitian.
- Support newborn screening; counsel parents of a child with PKU about the lifelong diet.
- Advise albino patients and families about sun protection and eye care.

## Remember

- Essential amino acids (+ 2 semi-essential): PVT TIM HALL; arginine and histidine are semi-essential.
- Purely ketogenic: leucine and lysine.
- Pepsin (stomach, activated by HCl); trypsin activated by enteropeptidase; rennin clots milk in infants.
- Transamination needs vitamin B6; urea is made only in the liver via the urea cycle.
- Glycine → haem, creatine, glutathione; tyrosine → catecholamines, thyroxine, melanin; tryptophan → serotonin, melatonin, niacin; histidine → histamine.
- PKU = phenylalanine hydroxylase defect (mousy odour, intellectual disability); alkaptonuria = urine darkens on standing; albinism = tyrosinase defect.
- Serum (about): total protein 6–8, albumin 3.5–5, globulin 2–3.5 g/dL; A:G ratio normally above 1 (about 1.5–2 : 1).
- Albumin keeps oncotic pressure; low albumin → oedema.
- Proteinuria > about 150 mg/day; Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma.
- Electrophoresis at pH 8.6: albumin fastest towards the anode; M band = myeloma; β–γ bridging = cirrhosis; α2 ↑ with albumin ↓ = nephrotic syndrome.

# Unit 4: Clinical enzymology

INC Unit IV (4 hours): isoenzymes — definition and properties; enzymes of diagnostic importance in liver diseases (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT), myocardial infarction (CK, cardiac troponins, AST, LDH), muscle diseases (CK, aldolase), bone diseases (ALP) and prostate cancer (PSA, ACP).

> Enzyme reference ranges depend heavily on the method, temperature and units used by each laboratory, so these notes describe *which* enzyme rises and *how much*, and do not give fixed normal values except where a figure is well established (marked "about").

## 4.1 Enzymes — a quick recap

**Enzymes** are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in the body without being used up. The substance acted on is the **substrate**. Many need a non-protein helper: a **coenzyme** (often a B-vitamin derivative, e.g. pyridoxal phosphate for transaminases) or a metal ion **cofactor** (Mg²⁺ for kinases, Zn²⁺).

Factors affecting enzyme activity: substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, temperature (optimum about 37 °C; high heat denatures), pH (each enzyme has an optimum — pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8), activators and inhibitors. Activity is reported in **units per litre (U/L or IU/L)**.

**Why plasma enzymes help diagnosis**

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Functional plasma enzymes** | Act in plasma; normally present in high amounts | Clotting factors (thrombin), lipoprotein lipase |
| **Non-functional plasma enzymes** | Work **inside cells**; only small amounts leak into plasma during normal cell turnover | ALT, AST, CK, LDH, ALP, GGT, amylase |

When cells are damaged or die, or their production is increased, their enzymes spill into the blood. The **rise** points to the **organ damaged**, and the **pattern over time** helps judge when damage happened and how much.

Other clinically useful enzymes outside this syllabus list: **amylase and lipase** (acute pancreatitis), **cholinesterase** (low in liver disease and organophosphate poisoning). Enzymes are also used as **drugs** (streptokinase, asparaginase) and as **reagents** in tests (glucose oxidase in glucose test strips, enzymes in ELISA).

## 4.2 Isoenzymes

**Definition**: isoenzymes (isozymes) are **different molecular forms of the same enzyme** that catalyse the **same reaction**, but differ in their structure and physical, chemical and immunological properties. They are made by different genes or by different combinations of sub-units, and are usually found in different tissues.

**Properties (ways in which isoenzymes differ)**

1. **Amino acid composition and structure** (different sub-units, e.g. H and M sub-units of LDH).
2. **Electrophoretic mobility** — they move different distances in electrophoresis; this is the commonest way to separate them.
3. **Tissue (organ) distribution** — each tissue has a typical isoenzyme; this gives **organ specificity** to a test.
4. **Kinetic properties** — different affinity for the substrate (Km) and maximum speed.
5. **Heat stability** — e.g. placental ALP is heat-stable, bone ALP is heat-labile.
6. **Response to inhibitors** — e.g. prostatic acid phosphatase is inhibited by tartrate.
7. **Immunological properties** — antibodies can tell them apart (used to measure CK-MB mass, troponins).
8. Sub-cellular location (cytoplasmic and mitochondrial forms of AST).

**Clinical value**: total enzyme activity tells you that cells are damaged somewhere; the isoenzyme tells you **which organ**.

### Important isoenzymes

**Creatine kinase (CK)** — a dimer of M (muscle) and B (brain) sub-units:

| Isoenzyme | Sub-units | Main tissue | Raised in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CK-1 (CK-BB) | BB | Brain, smooth muscle | Brain injury, stroke (rarely measured) |
| CK-2 (**CK-MB**) | MB | **Heart muscle** (heart has the highest share) | **Myocardial infarction**, myocarditis, after cardiac surgery |
| CK-3 (CK-MM) | MM | Skeletal muscle (most of normal serum CK) | Muscle injury, muscular dystrophy, IM injections, exercise |

**Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** — a tetramer of H (heart) and M (muscle) sub-units; five isoenzymes:

| Isoenzyme | Sub-units | Main tissue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LDH-1 | H4 | Heart, RBCs, kidney |
| LDH-2 | H3M | Heart, RBCs (normally the largest fraction in serum) |
| LDH-3 | H2M2 | Lungs, spleen, other tissues |
| LDH-4 | HM3 | Liver, skeletal muscle |
| LDH-5 | M4 | **Liver**, skeletal muscle |

Normally LDH-2 > LDH-1. After MI, LDH-1 rises above LDH-2 — the "**flipped LDH pattern**". LDH-5 rises in liver disease. LDH also rises in haemolysis (from RBCs), megaloblastic anaemia, many cancers; a haemolysed sample gives a falsely high LDH.

**Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)** isoenzymes: liver, bone, intestinal and placental (heat-stable; a similar heat-stable "Regan" isoenzyme appears in some cancers).

## 4.3 Enzymes in liver diseases — ALT, AST, ALP, GGT

| Enzyme | Where it comes from | Raised in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ALT** (alanine aminotransferase; old name SGPT) | Mainly **liver** cytoplasm → the **most liver-specific** of the four | Hepatocellular damage: acute **viral hepatitis** (very high — often more than 10 times the upper limit), drug- or toxin-induced hepatitis, fatty liver (mild), cirrhosis (mild or normal) |
| **AST** (aspartate aminotransferase; old name SGOT) | Liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, RBCs (cytoplasm and mitochondria) — **less specific** | Liver damage (as ALT), **myocardial infarction**, muscle injury, haemolysis |
| **ALP** (alkaline phosphatase) | Lining of the **bile canaliculi** (liver), bone (osteoblasts), placenta, intestine | **Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice** — gallstone in the bile duct, cancer of the head of the pancreas, intrahepatic cholestasis, liver secondaries — marked rise; only mild rise in hepatitis |
| **GGT** (γ-glutamyl transferase) | Liver (bile ducts), kidney, pancreas | **Alcohol** intake (sensitive marker of drinking), cholestasis (rises with ALP), drugs that induce liver enzymes (phenytoin, phenobarbital), fatty liver |

**Reading the pattern**

```text
Hepatocellular pattern (hepatitis):  ALT ↑↑↑, AST ↑↑↑, ALP mild ↑, GGT mild ↑
                                      ALT > AST in viral hepatitis
Cholestatic pattern (obstruction):   ALP ↑↑↑, GGT ↑↑↑, ALT/AST mild ↑, conjugated bilirubin ↑
Alcoholic liver disease:             AST : ALT ratio more than 2, GGT ↑↑
```

**Why GGT with ALP?** ALP rises in both bone and biliary disease. If GGT is also raised, the ALP is from the **liver**; if GGT is normal, think of **bone**.

## 4.4 Enzymes in myocardial infarction — CK, troponins, AST, LDH

When heart muscle dies, its proteins leak into blood in a typical **time sequence**. Today **cardiac troponins** are the preferred markers; AST and LDH are mostly of historical/teaching value but are still asked in exams.

| Marker | Starts to rise | Peaks | Returns to normal | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cardiac troponin I / T** | about 3–6 h (earlier with high-sensitivity tests) | about 12–24 h | **I: about 7–10 days; T: up to about 14 days** | **Most specific and sensitive** for heart muscle damage; the marker of choice; also detects a late-presenting MI |
| **CK-MB** | about 3–6 h | about 12–24 h | about 2–3 days | Good for detecting **re-infarction** (it returns to normal quickly) |
| Total CK | about 4–6 h | about 24 h | about 3–4 days | Not specific — also from skeletal muscle |
| **AST** | about 6–8 h | about 24–48 h | about 4–6 days | Not specific (liver, muscle) |
| **LDH** | about 12–24 h | about 2–3 days | about 8–14 days | Late marker; **LDH-1 > LDH-2 (flipped pattern)** |

```text
Height
of rise   Troponin ───────────────────────────────── (stays 7–14 days)
  ↑        CK-MB  ──────╲
  │       AST         ─────────╲
  │      LDH                ─────────────────╲
  └──────────────────────────────────────────→ time after chest pain
    0     6 h   12 h  24 h  2 d   3 d   5 d   7 d   14 d
  Order of rise:  troponin ≈ CK-MB → AST → LDH
  Order of fall:  CK-MB → AST → LDH and troponin (last)
```

**Troponins** are not enzymes; they are regulatory proteins of the heart's contraction apparatus (troponin T binds tropomyosin, troponin I inhibits contraction, troponin C binds calcium). Cardiac forms differ from skeletal forms, so tests are heart-specific. They are listed with enzymes because they are used the same way. Troponin can also rise in myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, severe sepsis and kidney failure, so it is read with the ECG and symptoms. **Myoglobin** rises earliest (1–3 h) but is not heart-specific.

## 4.5 Enzymes in muscle diseases — CK, aldolase

| Enzyme | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **CK (mainly CK-MM)** | The best enzyme for skeletal muscle damage. **Very high in Duchenne muscular dystrophy** (raised from early childhood, even before weakness; often raised in female carriers), polymyositis/dermatomyositis, crush injury and **rhabdomyolysis**, severe exercise, prolonged fits, IM injections, hypothyroidism. Normal in purely neurogenic weakness (e.g. myasthenia gravis, nerve disease) |
| **Aldolase** | A glycolytic enzyme; raised in muscular dystrophy and inflammatory muscle disease; less specific (also liver, RBCs) and now less used |

In rhabdomyolysis, myoglobin from damaged muscle can block kidney tubules → acute kidney injury; urine looks dark brown ("cola-coloured").

## 4.6 Enzymes in bone diseases — ALP

**Bone ALP** comes from **osteoblasts** (bone-forming cells), so it rises whenever bone formation is increased.

| Raised ALP — bone causes | Physiological rise |
| --- | --- |
| **Rickets** (children) and **osteomalacia** (adults) — vitamin D deficiency | **Growing children and adolescents** (growth spurt) |
| **Paget's disease of bone** — very high values | **Pregnancy** (placental ALP, third trimester) |
| **Bone secondaries** that form new bone (e.g. from prostate cancer) | Healing fractures |
| Hyperparathyroidism, osteogenic sarcoma | |

ALP is usually normal in osteoporosis and in multiple myeloma (bone destruction without new bone formation). Use GGT to tell bone ALP from liver ALP (4.3).

## 4.7 Enzymes in prostate cancer — PSA, ACP

| Marker | What it is | Clinical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **PSA (prostate-specific antigen)** | A protease (serine protease) made by prostate gland cells; keeps semen liquid | **Main marker** for screening (with digital rectal examination), diagnosis and follow-up of prostate cancer. Commonly a value above about **4 ng/mL** needs further evaluation (cut-offs vary with age). It is prostate-specific but **not cancer-specific**: also rises in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, urinary retention, after catheterisation, cystoscopy, prostate biopsy, digital rectal examination and ejaculation |
| **ACP (acid phosphatase)** | Phosphatase that works at acid pH; prostate is the richest source; also in RBCs, bone, platelets | **Prostatic ACP** (inhibited by **tartrate** — "tartrate-labile") rises when prostate cancer has **spread beyond the capsule, especially to bone**. Largely replaced by PSA. It is also found in semen (used in forensic work after alleged sexual assault) |

## 4.8 Collecting enzyme samples — nursing points

1. **Avoid haemolysis**: use a proper needle size, avoid prolonged tourniquet, do not shake the tube, send promptly. RBCs contain LDH, AST, ACP and potassium, so haemolysis gives falsely high values.
2. **Timing matters in suspected MI**: record the **time of onset of chest pain** and the time of each sample; troponin is often repeated after a few hours.
3. **Before PSA**: collect blood **before** a digital rectal examination, catheterisation or prostate procedure, or as advised (these raise PSA); note recent ejaculation or urinary retention.
4. **CK**: note recent IM injections, falls, fits, vigorous exercise or surgery — all raise CK.
5. Use the tube type the lab specifies, label with name, date and time, and send without delay; enzymes lose activity if left at room temperature.
6. Interpret results with clinical signs; tell the doctor at once about a rising troponin.

## Remember

- Non-functional plasma enzymes (ALT, AST, CK, LDH, ALP) act inside cells; a rise means cell damage or increased production.
- Isoenzymes: different forms of the same enzyme, same reaction; differ in structure, electrophoretic mobility, tissue distribution, Km, heat stability, inhibitors.
- CK: BB brain, MB heart, MM skeletal muscle. LDH: 5 isoenzymes; LDH-1 heart and RBCs, LDH-5 liver and muscle; flipped LDH-1 > LDH-2 after MI.
- Liver: ALT most liver-specific; ALT > AST in viral hepatitis; AST : ALT > 2 in alcoholic liver disease; ALP + GGT ↑↑ in obstructive jaundice; GGT ↑ with alcohol.
- MI: troponin is the marker of choice (rises 3–6 h, stays up to 7–14 days); CK-MB normal in 2–3 days (re-infarction); AST next; LDH last (normal by 8–14 days).
- Muscle disease: CK (very high in Duchenne dystrophy), aldolase.
- Bone: ALP ↑ in rickets, osteomalacia, Paget's, osteoblastic secondaries; normally high in children and pregnancy.
- Prostate: PSA (above about 4 ng/mL needs work-up; also raised in BPH, after rectal examination); prostatic ACP is tartrate-labile, raised in spread to bone.
- Avoid haemolysis — falsely high LDH, AST, ACP and potassium.

# Unit 5: Acid–base balance

INC Unit V (3 hours): pH — definition and normal value; regulation of blood pH by blood buffers, the lungs and the kidneys; arterial blood gas (ABG) normal values; acid–base disorders — types, definitions and causes. The INC assessment for this unit is short and very short answers, but this topic is used every day in wards and ICUs.

> ABG values below are approximate ("about") adult arterial values at sea level; laboratories and analysers print their own ranges.

## 5.1 Acids, bases and pH

- An **acid** gives up hydrogen ions (H⁺) — a proton donor (e.g. carbonic acid H2CO3, lactic acid, ketone acids).
- A **base** accepts hydrogen ions — a proton acceptor (e.g. bicarbonate HCO3⁻).
- **pH** is the **negative logarithm (to base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration**:

```text
pH = −log10 [H⁺]
```

Because the scale is logarithmic and negative:

- a **lower pH = more H⁺ = more acidic**; a higher pH = fewer H⁺ = more alkaline;
- a change of **1 pH unit = a tenfold change** in [H⁺]; even a fall from 7.4 to 7.1 roughly doubles [H⁺].

**Normal blood pH: about 7.35–7.45 (mean 7.4)** — slightly alkaline.

| pH | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Below 7.35 | **Acidaemia** (the process causing it is acidosis) |
| 7.35–7.45 | Normal |
| Above 7.45 | **Alkalaemia** (the process is alkalosis) |
| Below about 6.8 or above about 7.8 | Usually not compatible with life |

**Why pH must be held steady**: enzymes, ion channels, oxygen carriage by haemoglobin, heart rhythm and nerve function all depend on pH. Acidosis depresses the brain (confusion, coma) and the heart; alkalosis makes nerves irritable (tingling, tetany, fits).

**Where the acid comes from**: the body produces acid constantly — a very large amount of CO2 (volatile acid, removed by the lungs) from metabolism, and a smaller amount of **fixed (non-volatile) acids** such as sulphuric acid (from sulphur amino acids), phosphoric acid, lactic acid and ketone acids, which must be removed by the kidneys.

## 5.2 Three lines of defence

```text
Acid load
   ↓
1. BLOOD BUFFERS   — act in seconds; limit the change but do not remove acid
   ↓
2. LUNGS           — act in minutes; blow off or retain CO2 (carbonic acid)
   ↓
3. KIDNEYS         — act over hours to days; excrete H⁺ and make/reabsorb HCO3⁻;
                     the only route that removes fixed acid permanently
```

## 5.3 Blood buffers

A **buffer** is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt (conjugate base) that **resists a change in pH** when an acid or base is added.

| Buffer system | Where | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bicarbonate buffer** (H2CO3 / NaHCO3) | Plasma, ECF | **Most important buffer of blood/ECF** — both parts can be adjusted: CO2 by the lungs, HCO3⁻ by the kidneys |
| **Phosphate buffer** (NaH2PO4 / Na2HPO4) | Inside cells and in **urine (renal tubules)** | Main buffer of intracellular fluid and of tubular fluid |
| **Protein buffer** | Plasma proteins and cell proteins | Side chains (especially histidine) take up or release H⁺ |
| **Haemoglobin buffer** | Red blood cells | **Most important buffer of the H⁺ produced from CO2 carriage**; deoxygenated Hb is a better buffer, so it takes up H⁺ in tissues |

**How the bicarbonate buffer works**

```text
CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO3⁻          (carbonic anhydrase speeds the first step)

Strong acid added:  HCl + NaHCO3  →  NaCl + H2CO3  →  H2O + CO2 (breathed out)
Strong base added:  NaOH + H2CO3  →  NaHCO3 + H2O   (excess HCO3⁻ excreted by kidney)
```

**Henderson–Hasselbalch equation** (for the bicarbonate buffer):

```text
pH = pKa + log [HCO3⁻] / [H2CO3]
   = 6.1 + log [HCO3⁻] / (0.03 × pCO2)

Normal: HCO3⁻ 24 mmol/L ; H2CO3 = 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L
Ratio = 24 / 1.2 = 20 : 1  →  log 20 = 1.3  →  pH = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4
```

**Key idea**: blood pH depends on the **ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid (20 : 1)**, not on their absolute amounts. HCO3⁻ is the **metabolic (kidney) component**; pCO2 is the **respiratory (lung) component**. If one changes, the body tries to change the other in the same direction to bring the ratio back towards 20 : 1 — this is **compensation**.

## 5.4 Respiratory regulation

- CO2 is an acid-forming gas (it forms H2CO3). The **respiratory centre** in the medulla (and chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies and the brain stem) responds to a rise in pCO2 or H⁺.
- **Acidosis → faster and deeper breathing** → more CO2 blown off → pH rises (seen as **Kussmaul breathing** in diabetic ketoacidosis).
- **Alkalosis → slower, shallower breathing** → CO2 retained → pH falls.
- Fast (minutes), but can only remove volatile acid and can only partly correct a metabolic problem (limited, because slowing breathing too far causes hypoxia).

## 5.5 Renal regulation

The kidney is slow (hours to 2–3 days) but is the only organ that can **excrete fixed acid** and **regenerate bicarbonate**. Tubular cells contain carbonic anhydrase, which makes H⁺ and HCO3⁻ from CO2 and water.

| Mechanism | Where | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. **Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate** | Mainly proximal tubule | H⁺ secreted into tubular fluid combines with filtered HCO3⁻ → CO2 + H2O → reabsorbed; a new HCO3⁻ returns to blood — **no net acid excreted, but bicarbonate is saved** |
| 2. **Excretion of titratable acid** | Distal tubule | Secreted H⁺ is buffered by **phosphate** in urine (HPO4²⁻ + H⁺ → H2PO4⁻); a new HCO3⁻ is added to blood for each H⁺ |
| 3. **Excretion of ammonium (NH4⁺)** | Proximal and distal tubules | Tubular cells make **ammonia (NH3) from glutamine**; NH3 traps H⁺ as NH4⁺ in urine — the **main way to increase acid excretion in chronic acidosis** |
| 4. Urine acidification | Collecting ducts | Urine pH can range from about 4.5 to 8 |

In acidosis the kidney excretes more H⁺ (more acid urine) and returns more bicarbonate to blood; in alkalosis it excretes bicarbonate (alkaline urine).

## 5.6 Arterial blood gas (ABG) — normal values

| Parameter | Normal (arterial, about) | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH | **7.35–7.45** | Overall acid–base state |
| PaCO2 | **35–45 mmHg** | Respiratory component (lungs) |
| HCO3⁻ (bicarbonate) | **22–26 mmol/L (mEq/L)** | Metabolic component (kidneys) |
| PaO2 | **80–100 mmHg** (on room air) | Oxygenation (not an acid–base value) |
| SaO2 | **95–100%** | Saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen |
| Base excess | **about −2 to +2 mmol/L** | Negative = metabolic acidosis; positive = metabolic alkalosis |
| Anion gap | **about 8–16 mmol/L** (method-dependent) | Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻); see 5.8 |

Venous blood has a slightly lower pH, higher pCO2 and much lower pO2 — ABG must be **arterial**.

## 5.7 Acid–base disorders — types, definitions, causes

| Disorder | Definition | Primary change | pH | Compensation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Metabolic acidosis** | Fall in pH due to a primary **fall in HCO3⁻** (gain of fixed acid or loss of bicarbonate) | HCO3⁻ ↓ | ↓ | Lungs: hyperventilation → PaCO2 ↓ |
| **Metabolic alkalosis** | Rise in pH due to a primary **rise in HCO3⁻** (loss of H⁺ or gain of bicarbonate) | HCO3⁻ ↑ | ↑ | Lungs: hypoventilation → PaCO2 ↑ (limited) |
| **Respiratory acidosis** | Fall in pH due to a primary **rise in PaCO2** (under-ventilation, CO2 retention) | PaCO2 ↑ | ↓ | Kidneys: retain HCO3⁻ → HCO3⁻ ↑ |
| **Respiratory alkalosis** | Rise in pH due to a primary **fall in PaCO2** (over-ventilation) | PaCO2 ↓ | ↑ | Kidneys: excrete HCO3⁻ → HCO3⁻ ↓ |

Memory aid: **ROME — Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.** In respiratory disorders pH and PaCO2 move in **opposite** directions; in metabolic disorders pH and HCO3⁻ move in the **same** direction.

### Causes

**Metabolic acidosis**

- *High anion gap* (an extra acid is added): **diabetic ketoacidosis**, starvation ketosis, **lactic acidosis** (shock, severe hypoxia, cardiac arrest, sepsis), **renal failure** (retained sulphate, phosphate), poisoning (e.g. methanol, salicylate)
- *Normal anion gap* (bicarbonate lost, chloride retained): **severe diarrhoea**, intestinal fistula or ileostomy loss, renal tubular acidosis, ureterosigmoid diversion, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor drugs

**Metabolic alkalosis**

- Loss of H⁺: **prolonged vomiting**, **continuous nasogastric aspiration**, pyloric stenosis (loss of stomach HCl)
- Diuretics (thiazide and loop), **hypokalaemia**
- Excess mineralocorticoid: Cushing's syndrome, hyperaldosteronism
- Excess alkali intake: antacids/bicarbonate, massive transfusion (citrate → bicarbonate)

**Respiratory acidosis** (CO2 retention)

- Lung disease: **COPD** (chronic bronchitis, emphysema), severe asthma, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema
- Depressed respiratory centre: overdose of opioids or sedatives, general anaesthesia, head injury, stroke
- Weak breathing muscles or chest wall: Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, polio, spinal cord injury, chest injury, severe obesity
- Airway obstruction, inadequate mechanical ventilation

**Respiratory alkalosis** (CO2 washed out)

- **Hyperventilation** due to anxiety, panic, pain, fever
- High altitude, hypoxia, severe anaemia
- Early salicylate poisoning, liver failure, sepsis, pregnancy (mild, normal), brain lesions
- Excess mechanical ventilation

### Main clinical features

| Disorder | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Metabolic acidosis | Deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing, headache, confusion, drowsiness, low BP, arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia |
| Metabolic alkalosis | Slow shallow breathing, muscle cramps, tingling, tetany, arrhythmia, hypokalaemia |
| Respiratory acidosis | Breathlessness, headache, flushed warm skin, drowsiness ("CO2 narcosis"), confusion |
| Respiratory alkalosis | Light-headedness, tingling around the mouth and fingers, carpopedal spasm (low ionised calcium), palpitations |

## 5.8 Anion gap

```text
Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻)
Example:   140 − (104 + 24) = 12 mmol/L  (normal, about 8–16)
```

It represents unmeasured anions (mainly albumin, phosphate, sulphate, organic acids). A **raised anion gap** in metabolic acidosis means an extra acid has been added (ketones, lactate, uraemic acids, poisons); a **normal anion gap** means bicarbonate has been lost (diarrhoea) and replaced by chloride (hyperchloraemic acidosis).

## 5.9 Reading an ABG — simple steps

1. **pH**: below 7.35 = acidaemia; above 7.45 = alkalaemia.
2. **PaCO2**: does it explain the pH? (High PaCO2 with low pH → respiratory acidosis; low PaCO2 with high pH → respiratory alkalosis.)
3. **HCO3⁻**: does it explain the pH? (Low HCO3⁻ with low pH → metabolic acidosis; high HCO3⁻ with high pH → metabolic alkalosis.)
4. **Compensation**: the other value moving in the same direction as the primary one = compensation. Partly compensated if pH is still abnormal; fully compensated if pH is back in the normal range (usually on the side of the primary problem). Compensation never over-corrects.
5. **Oxygenation**: PaO2 and SaO2.
6. In metabolic acidosis, calculate the **anion gap**.

**Worked examples**

| pH | PaCO2 | HCO3⁻ | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.25 | 30 | 14 | Metabolic acidosis, partly compensated (e.g. DKA) |
| 7.52 | 46 | 36 | Metabolic alkalosis, partly compensated (e.g. vomiting) |
| 7.28 | 60 | 27 | Acute respiratory acidosis (e.g. opioid overdose) |
| 7.36 | 58 | 32 | Respiratory acidosis, compensated (e.g. chronic COPD) |
| 7.50 | 28 | 22 | Acute respiratory alkalosis (e.g. anxiety hyperventilation) |

## 5.10 Nursing points

**Collecting an arterial blood sample (steps with reasons)**

1. Check the order, explain to the patient, note whether on oxygen (FiO2) and the temperature. *Reason*: results are read against oxygen given.
2. For the radial artery, do the **modified Allen test** (compress both radial and ulnar arteries, ask the patient to clench and open the hand, release the ulnar — colour should return within about 5–15 seconds). *Reason*: confirms ulnar circulation to the hand if the radial artery is damaged.
3. Use a **heparinised** ABG syringe with the right needle; follow aseptic technique. *Reason*: prevents clotting.
4. After the sample, **expel air bubbles at once** and cap the syringe. *Reason*: air changes PaO2 and PaCO2.
5. **Apply firm pressure for at least 5 minutes** (longer if on anticoagulants). *Reason*: prevents haematoma.
6. Label and send **immediately** (or on ice if a delay is unavoidable, as the lab advises). *Reason*: cells keep using O2 and making CO2.

**Other nursing links**: count respiratory rate and depth (Kussmaul breathing suggests metabolic acidosis); be careful with high-flow oxygen in chronic CO2 retainers (COPD) and watch for drowsiness; record vomiting, NG aspirate and diarrhoea losses (they cause alkalosis and acidosis respectively); calm and coach a hyperventilating patient to breathe slowly; watch potassium, which moves out of cells in acidosis and into cells in alkalosis.

## Remember

- pH = −log [H⁺]; normal blood pH about 7.35–7.45; one pH unit = tenfold change in [H⁺].
- Buffers act in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys in hours to days.
- Bicarbonate buffer is the main blood buffer; haemoglobin buffers H⁺ from CO2; phosphate buffers urine and cells.
- HCO3⁻ : H2CO3 ratio 20 : 1 keeps pH 7.4 (pH = 6.1 + log 20).
- Kidney: reabsorbs bicarbonate, excretes titratable acid (phosphate) and ammonium (main response in chronic acidosis).
- ABG (about): pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, HCO3⁻ 22–26 mmol/L, PaO2 80–100 mmHg, SaO2 95–100%.
- ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.
- Metabolic acidosis: DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea. Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting, NG aspiration, diuretics, hypokalaemia.
- Respiratory acidosis: COPD, respiratory depression. Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation, high altitude.
- Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻), about 8–16; high in ketoacidosis and lactic acidosis.

# Unit 6: Heme catabolism, jaundice and organ function tests

This notes file joins two small INC units:

- **INC Unit VI — Heme catabolism (2 hours)**: haem degradation pathway; jaundice — types, causes, urine and blood investigations (van den Bergh test).
- **INC Unit VII — Organ function tests (3 hours)**: renal, liver and thyroid function tests — biochemical parameters and normal values only.

They are joined because bilirubin is the link: the liver function tests begin with serum bilirubin, and jaundice is read from the same tests. Both units are assessed by short and very short answers.

> All normal values here are approximate ("about") adult values. Each laboratory prints its own reference range, which depends on its method and units; always read the report against that range.

## 6.1 Haem and its breakdown — why it matters

**Haem** is an iron-containing porphyrin ring (protoporphyrin + Fe²⁺). It is part of haemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes and catalase. About 80–85% of haem broken down each day comes from **old red blood cells** (life span about **120 days**); the rest from immature RBCs in the marrow and other haem proteins.

## 6.2 Haem degradation pathway

```text
OLD RBCs (about 120 days) — taken up by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system
                            (mainly spleen; also liver Kupffer cells, bone marrow)
        │
   Haemoglobin → Globin (→ amino acids, reused) + HAEM
        │
        │  haem oxygenase (needs O2, NADPH)
        ↓
   BILIVERDIN (green)  +  Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ (→ stored as ferritin / reused)  +  CO (breathed out)
        │
        │  biliverdin reductase (NADPH)
        ↓
   BILIRUBIN (orange-yellow) = UNCONJUGATED bilirubin
        │   insoluble in water; carried in blood bound to ALBUMIN
        │   (so it is NOT filtered by the kidney and not found in urine)
        ↓
   LIVER CELL: uptake → CONJUGATION with glucuronic acid
        │   enzyme: UDP-glucuronyl transferase
        ↓
   BILIRUBIN DIGLUCURONIDE = CONJUGATED bilirubin (water-soluble)
        │   secreted actively into bile canaliculi (rate-limiting step)
        ↓
   BILE → INTESTINE
        │   bacteria remove glucuronic acid and reduce bilirubin
        ↓
   UROBILINOGEN (colourless)
        ├─ most → oxidised to STERCOBILINOGEN → STERCOBILIN (brown colour of stool)
        └─ some → reabsorbed into portal blood → most re-excreted by liver in bile
                  (enterohepatic urobilinogen cycle); a small amount → kidney →
                  URINE UROBILINOGEN → oxidised to UROBILIN (yellow colour of urine)
```

**Key differences between the two forms**

| Feature | Unconjugated (indirect) | Conjugated (direct) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solubility | Fat-soluble, not water-soluble | Water-soluble |
| Transport in blood | Bound to albumin | Loosely bound/free |
| In urine | **Never** (too tightly bound, not filtered) | Appears when its blood level rises |
| Toxicity | Can enter the brain of newborns → **kernicterus** | Not toxic to brain |
| van den Bergh | **Indirect** reaction (needs alcohol) | **Direct** reaction |

**Normal serum bilirubin (about)**: total **0.2–1.2 mg/dL** (often quoted 0.3–1.0); conjugated (direct) **up to about 0.3 mg/dL**; unconjugated (indirect) = total − direct.

## 6.3 Jaundice

**Definition**: yellow colour of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes due to a raised serum bilirubin. Jaundice is usually **visible when total bilirubin is above about 2–3 mg/dL** (first seen in the sclera, in daylight). A level above normal but below this, with no visible yellow colour, is **latent (subclinical) jaundice**.

### Types and causes

| Type | Basic problem | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pre-hepatic (haemolytic)** | Too much bilirubin made — more than the normal liver can conjugate | Haemolytic anaemias: hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, **G6PD deficiency**, malaria, **mismatched blood transfusion**, **Rh/ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn**, large haematoma breakdown |
| **Hepatic (hepatocellular)** | Liver cells damaged — both uptake/conjugation and excretion are faulty | **Viral hepatitis** (A, B, C, E), alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced hepatitis (e.g. some anti-TB drugs, paracetamol overdose), leptospirosis, liver cancer; inherited conjugation defects — **Gilbert's syndrome** (mild), Crigler–Najjar syndrome (severe), Dubin–Johnson and Rotor syndromes (excretion defects) |
| **Post-hepatic (obstructive / cholestatic)** | Bile cannot flow from liver to gut; conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood | **Gallstone in the common bile duct**, **carcinoma of the head of the pancreas**, cholangiocarcinoma, stricture of the bile duct, enlarged nodes at the porta hepatis, biliary atresia in infants, intrahepatic cholestasis (drugs, pregnancy) |

**Physiological jaundice of the newborn**: appears after 24 hours, usually on days 2–3, and fades within about 1–2 weeks. Causes: high RBC breakdown (shorter RBC life, high RBC count at birth) and immature liver conjugating enzyme (UDP-glucuronyl transferase). It is unconjugated. Jaundice in the **first 24 hours**, rising rapidly, or lasting beyond 2 weeks is **pathological** and needs investigation. Very high unconjugated bilirubin can cause **kernicterus** (brain damage); **phototherapy** changes bilirubin into water-soluble forms that can be excreted.

### Laboratory findings in the three types

| Test | Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) | Hepatic | Post-hepatic (obstructive) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serum unconjugated bilirubin | **↑↑** | ↑ | Normal or slight ↑ |
| Serum conjugated bilirubin | Normal | ↑ | **↑↑** |
| van den Bergh reaction | **Indirect** positive | **Biphasic** | **Direct** positive |
| **Urine bilirubin** (bile pigment) | **Absent** ("acholuric" jaundice) | Present | **Present** (dark, tea-coloured urine) |
| **Urine urobilinogen** | **↑↑** | Variable (↑ early, may ↓ at peak cholestasis) | **Absent** (no bile reaches the gut) |
| Urine bile salts | Absent | May be present | **Present** |
| Stool colour | Dark (more stercobilin) | Normal or pale | **Clay-coloured, pale** |
| ALT / AST | Normal | **Markedly ↑** | Mild ↑ |
| ALP / GGT | Normal | Mild ↑ | **Markedly ↑** |
| Other | Anaemia, ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin | Prothrombin time may be prolonged | Itching (bile salts in skin), slow pulse, fat malabsorption, vitamin K deficiency (prolonged PT corrected by vitamin K) |

## 6.4 Investigations

### Blood: van den Bergh test

**Principle**: bilirubin reacts with **diazotised sulphanilic acid (diazo reagent)** to form a **reddish-purple azobilirubin**, whose colour intensity is measured.

| Reaction | What happens | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Direct** | Colour appears **at once** in watery solution (no alcohol needed) | **Conjugated** (water-soluble) bilirubin — obstructive jaundice |
| **Indirect** | Colour appears **only after adding alcohol (methanol)**, which dissolves unconjugated bilirubin | **Unconjugated** bilirubin — haemolytic jaundice |
| **Biphasic** | Some colour at once, deepening after alcohol | Both raised — hepatic jaundice |

In modern labs the same diazo principle is used on analysers to report **total and direct bilirubin**; indirect = total − direct.

### Urine tests

| Substance | Test | Positive result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bile pigments (bilirubin)** | **Fouchet's test** (barium chloride + Fouchet's reagent: ferric chloride in trichloroacetic acid); also dipstick | **Green/blue** colour |
| | Gmelin's test (nitric acid) | Play of colours (rings) |
| **Bile salts** | **Hay's test** — sprinkle fine **sulphur powder** on the urine | Sulphur **sinks** (bile salts lower the surface tension); normally it floats |
| **Urobilinogen** | **Ehrlich's test** (Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent — p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde); use **fresh** urine | **Cherry-red** colour (increased) |

**Nursing tips for urine tests**: test **fresh** urine (urobilinogen oxidises to urobilin and bilirubin breaks down in light); protect the sample from light; note the colour of urine and stool.

## 6.5 Organ function tests — renal function tests (RFT)

The kidneys excrete nitrogenous wastes, keep water, electrolytes and acid–base balance, and make erythropoietin, renin and active vitamin D.

**Blood parameters (about)**

| Parameter | Normal (about) | Rises in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Blood urea** | 15–40 mg/dL (BUN about 7–20 mg/dL) | Kidney failure; also dehydration, high-protein diet, GI bleeding, catabolic states (pre-renal); falls in liver failure, pregnancy |
| **Serum creatinine** | about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL (slightly lower in women) | **Kidney failure** — a better index of GFR than urea, as it is little affected by diet; also with large muscle mass |
| **Serum uric acid** | about 3.5–7 mg/dL (men), 2.5–6 mg/dL (women) | Gout, kidney failure, leukaemia and chemotherapy (cell breakdown), pre-eclampsia |
| Serum sodium | 135–145 mmol/L | — |
| Serum potassium | 3.5–5.0 mmol/L | **Hyperkalaemia in kidney failure** (dangerous to the heart) |
| Serum chloride | about 96–106 mmol/L | — |
| Serum bicarbonate | 22–26 mmol/L | Falls in kidney failure (metabolic acidosis) |
| Serum calcium (total) | about 8.5–10.5 mg/dL | Falls in chronic kidney disease |
| Serum phosphate | about 2.5–4.5 mg/dL | Rises in chronic kidney disease |
| BUN : creatinine ratio | about 10–20 : 1 | > 20 suggests pre-renal cause (dehydration, bleeding) |

**Clearance and GFR (about)**

| Test | Normal (about) |
| --- | --- |
| **Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** | about 120 mL/min (90–120 mL/min/1.73 m² is normal; it falls with age) |
| **Creatinine clearance** | about 90–130 mL/min (uses timed urine + serum creatinine: C = U × V / P) |
| **eGFR** | Calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex; above 90 mL/min/1.73 m² is normal; below 60 for 3 months or more suggests chronic kidney disease |
| Urea clearance | about 75 mL/min (maximum clearance) — older test, rarely used |
| Inulin clearance | Gold standard for GFR (research use) |

**Urine parameters (about)**

| Parameter | Normal (about) |
| --- | --- |
| Volume | 1–2 litres per day (polyuria above about 3 L/day; oliguria below about 400 mL/day; anuria below about 100 mL/day) |
| Specific gravity | 1.003–1.030 (concentrating ability: early-morning sample usually above 1.020) |
| pH | about 4.5–8 (average about 6) |
| Protein | less than about 150 mg/day; albumin less than about 30 mg/day |
| Glucose, ketones, bilirubin, blood | Absent |
| Deposits | A few epithelial cells; occasional RBCs and pus cells; casts and crystals may indicate disease |

**Formula for clearance**

```text
Clearance (mL/min) = (U × V) / P
U = urine concentration, V = urine flow (mL/min), P = plasma concentration
Example: urine creatinine 100 mg/dL, urine flow 1.2 mL/min, plasma creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
         → clearance = (100 × 1.2) / 1.0 = 120 mL/min
```

## 6.6 Liver function tests (LFT)

| Group | Parameter | Normal (about) | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Excretory function | **Serum bilirubin** — total / direct | 0.2–1.2 / up to 0.3 mg/dL | Jaundice and its type |
| | Urine bilirubin, urobilinogen, bile salts | Bilirubin absent; urobilinogen trace | Type of jaundice (6.3) |
| Liver cell damage | **ALT** (SGPT) | about 7–40 U/L* | Hepatocellular damage |
| | **AST** (SGOT) | about 8–40 U/L* | Hepatocellular damage (less specific) |
| Cholestasis | **ALP** | about 40–130 U/L* in adults (higher in children, pregnancy) | Obstruction, bone disease |
| | **GGT** | about 10–50 U/L* (higher in men) | Cholestasis, alcohol |
| Synthetic function | **Total serum protein** | 6–8 g/dL | — |
| | **Albumin** | 3.5–5.0 g/dL | Falls in chronic liver disease (long half-life, about 20 days) |
| | Globulin, A:G ratio | 2–3.5 g/dL; ratio above 1 | Reversed A:G in cirrhosis |
| | **Prothrombin time (PT) / INR** | PT about 11–14 s; INR about 1 | Prolonged in liver failure (clotting factors made in liver; short half-life — earliest sign of failing synthesis) |
| Others | Blood ammonia | Low; method-dependent | Rises in liver failure / hepatic encephalopathy |

\*Enzyme ranges differ the most between laboratories — always use the printed range.

**Patterns**: hepatocellular damage → ALT/AST ↑↑; cholestasis → ALP/GGT ↑↑ and direct bilirubin ↑; chronic liver disease (cirrhosis) → albumin ↓, globulin ↑, PT prolonged.

## 6.7 Thyroid function tests (TFT)

```text
Hypothalamus → TRH → Anterior pituitary → TSH → Thyroid → T4 (mostly) and T3
       ↑_______________ negative feedback by T4/T3 __________________|
```

Most T4 and T3 in blood is bound to proteins (mainly thyroxine-binding globulin); only the small **free** fraction is active, so **free T4 and free T3** are better tests than total levels.

| Parameter | Normal (about) |
| --- | --- |
| **TSH** | about 0.4–4.5 mIU/L (some labs 0.5–5) |
| **Total T4** | about 5–12 µg/dL |
| **Free T4 (FT4)** | about 0.8–1.8 ng/dL |
| **Total T3** | about 80–200 ng/dL |
| **Free T3 (FT3)** | about 2.3–4.2 pg/mL |
| Anti-TPO antibodies | Negative / low (raised in autoimmune thyroid disease — Hashimoto's) |

Values in pregnancy and in newborns differ; labs give trimester- and age-specific ranges.

**Interpretation**

| Condition | TSH | Free T4 / T3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary hypothyroidism** (thyroid fails — iodine deficiency, Hashimoto's, after surgery/radio-iodine) | **↑** | **↓** |
| Subclinical hypothyroidism | ↑ | Normal |
| **Primary hyperthyroidism** (Graves' disease, toxic nodule) | **↓** (suppressed) | **↑** |
| Secondary hypothyroidism (pituitary failure) | ↓ or inappropriately normal | ↓ |
| T3 toxicosis | ↓ | T4 normal, T3 ↑ |

**TSH is the best single screening test** for thyroid function (the pituitary responds to small changes in thyroid hormone). **Newborn screening** for congenital hypothyroidism (heel-prick TSH or T4) prevents intellectual disability (cretinism) because treatment started early works.

## 6.8 Application in nursing

- Inspect the sclera in daylight for jaundice; note urine (dark) and stool (pale) colour.
- In newborns, watch for jaundice in the first 24 hours; during phototherapy cover the eyes and genitals, turn the baby, keep hydration and temperature, check bilirubin as ordered.
- Relieve itching in obstructive jaundice (cool bath, trimmed nails, prescribed lotions); watch for bleeding (vitamin K deficiency) and check PT before procedures such as liver biopsy.
- Collect correct samples: fresh, light-protected urine for bilirubin/urobilinogen; 24-hour urine for creatinine clearance (discard first void, collect all for 24 h including the last, keep cool); fasting is not needed for most RFT/LFT but follow lab rules.
- Monitor intake–output, weight and potassium in kidney failure; report a rising creatinine or potassium.
- Thyroid tests: note drugs (thyroxine, steroids, amiodarone) and pregnancy on the request form.

## Remember

- RBC life about 120 days; haem → biliverdin (haem oxygenase) → bilirubin (biliverdin reductase); iron reused, CO breathed out.
- Unconjugated bilirubin travels on albumin, never appears in urine; conjugated in liver by UDP-glucuronyl transferase (bilirubin diglucuronide).
- Gut bacteria → urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool colour) and urine urobilin.
- Serum bilirubin about 0.2–1.2 mg/dL; direct up to about 0.3; jaundice visible above about 2–3 mg/dL.
- Haemolytic: indirect ↑, urine bilirubin absent, urobilinogen ↑. Obstructive: direct ↑, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen absent, clay stools, ALP ↑↑. Hepatic: biphasic, ALT/AST ↑↑.
- van den Bergh: diazo reagent → purple azobilirubin; direct = conjugated; indirect needs alcohol.
- Urine tests: Fouchet's (bile pigments), Hay's sulphur test (bile salts), Ehrlich's (urobilinogen).
- RFT (about): urea 15–40 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL, uric acid 3.5–7 mg/dL (men), GFR about 120 mL/min, urine 1–2 L/day, specific gravity 1.003–1.030.
- LFT: bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, total protein, albumin 3.5–5 g/dL, PT/INR.
- TFT: TSH about 0.4–4.5 mIU/L; primary hypothyroidism TSH ↑ T4 ↓; hyperthyroidism TSH ↓ T4/T3 ↑; TSH is the best screening test.
